MD_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-0:
This is the Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda beginning with the words, 'Brahmā among the gods'. At the very outset, by way of praising the vidyā itself, the Upaniṣad announces its sambandha — the connection in the form of the unbroken succession of teachers (paramparā) who have transmitted this knowledge. The implication is that this vidyā has been obtained through great labour by an exalted lineage of teachers, since it serves as the means to the supreme human end (paramapuruṣārtha). To kindle the listener's interest, the Upaniṣad first magnifies the vidyā by praise; for once a vidyā has been made attractive through eulogy, students will undertake it with reverence. As for the prayojana — the relation of means and end attaching to this vidyā — that will be stated later in such passages as 'the knot of the heart is sundered' (Mu.U. 2.2.9).

Here it is also indicated, in the very utterance of the text, that the so‑called aparā — the vidyā designated by the Ṛgveda and the rest, whose sole purport is injunction and prohibition — has no power to remove the defects of avidyā which are the cause of saṃsāra. Having said this, the Upaniṣad proceeds to divide vidyā into parā and aparā, and then by passages such as 'dwelling within avidyā' (Mu.U. 1.2.8) it shows the futility of mere ritual. Thereafter, in 'having examined the worlds' (Mu.U. 1.2.12) and the like, it sets forth the brahmavidyā which is the means to the attainment of the Supreme — a means that presupposes complete vairāgya towards every object attainable by any other means, and which is to be obtained only by the grace of the guru.

The prayojana, the result, is repeatedly proclaimed: 'He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman alone' (Mu.U. 3.2.9), and 'all, become supremely immortal, are wholly liberated' (Mu.U. 3.2.6). Although in the matter of mere knowledge every āśrama may have adhikāra, yet brahmavidyā issues in mokṣa only when it is grounded in saṃnyāsa — not when it is yoked together with karma. This the text shows by saying 'practising the mendicant's life' (Mu.U. 1.2.11) and 'through the yoga of saṃnyāsa' (Mu.U. 3.2.6). And there is, besides, an outright contradiction between vidyā and karma. The vision of the non‑duality of Brahman and the Self can never be conjoined with karma, not even in dream; for vidyā has no fixed time, no determinate occasioning cause, and so it does not admit of being confined to a particular interval — whereas karma is precisely a thing of stipulated time and occasion.

As for the linga sometimes adduced — that even householders are seen as transmitters of brahmavidyā — that linga has no power to overthrow the well‑established nyāya. Not by a hundred injunctions can darkness and light be made to coexist in one place; how much less by mere lingas alone! Thus the refuted Mīmāṃsaka view, which would conjoin jñāna with karma, cannot stand. Therefore, the sambandha and prayojana having been thus determined, a brief commentary upon this Upaniṣad is now begun. Those who, taking it to themselves with śraddhā and bhakti, draw near to this brahmavidyā — for them it slays utterly the whole crowd of evils such as conception, birth, old age and disease, and either leads them to the supreme Brahman or else completely beats down and destroys avidyā which is the very root of saṃsāra. Such is the force of upa‑ni‑ṣad, recalled from the root sad preceded by upa and ni — meaning loosening, leading near, and laying low.
MD_C01_S01_V01: Brahmā arose first among the gods, the maker of all, the protector of the world. He proclaimed the brahmavidyā, the foundation of all knowledge, to his eldest son Atharvan. (1)
MD_C01_S01_V01::block-0:
Brahman here means 'great' — the one who, by dharma, jñāna, vairāgya and aiśvarya, surpasses all others; pari‑bṛḍha, vast. Among the devas — those endowed with effulgence such as Indra and the rest — he is prathama, foremost in qualities; or prathama in the sense of being first in the order of manifestation. He came forth (sambabhūva) — that is, became fully manifest, and that by his own independent power. The intent is that he did not arise in the way that other transmigrants are born under the constraint of dharma and adharma; for the Smṛti says, 'He who is beyond the senses, ungraspable...' (Manu 1.7).

Of this whole jagat he is the maker (kartā), the producer; and of the produced bhuvana he is the gopā, the protector. These epithets are appended in praise of Brahmā for the sake of glorifying the vidyā. He, that Brahmā of such celebrated greatness, taught the brahmavidyā — the vidyā of Brahman, the Paramātman; for the qualifying clause to come, 'whereby the imperishable Puruṣa, the satya, is known' (Mu.U. 1.2.13), shows it pertains to the Paramātman. Or it is brahmavidyā in the sense that it was first uttered by Brahmā, the eldest born from the Word.

This vidyā he proclaims as sarvavidyā‑pratiṣṭhā — the basis of all vidyās; for it is the cause of the manifestation of every other vidyā, hence their āśraya. Or, the vastu which is to be known by every other vidyā becomes known through this one alone, as the Śruti says, 'whereby the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known' (Cha.U. 6.1.3). 'Foundation of all knowledge' is itself a stuti, a mode of praise of this vidyā. Atharvan was the eldest son: in one of the manifold modes of Brahmā's creation, Atharvan was created first at the head; therefore the eldest son. To him, this eldest son, Brahmā proclaimed it.
MD_C01_S01_V02: That brahmavidyā which Brahmā taught to Atharvan, Atharvan in turn imparted of old to Aṅgir. He proclaimed it to Bhāradvāja Satyavaha, and Bhāradvāja gave to Aṅgiras the parāvarā vidyā. (2)
MD_C01_S01_V02::block-0: That brahmavidyā which Brahmā imparted to Atharvan — the very one received from Brahmā — Atharvan of old, that is, in former time, taught to one named Aṅgir. That Aṅgir then proclaimed it to Bhāradvāja, of the Bharadvāja gotra, named Satyavaha; and Bhāradvāja, in turn, conveyed it to Aṅgiras, his own disciple — or son. The vidyā is called parāvarā either because it has come down from one teacher to another in succession (param param avareṇa avareṇa prāptā), or because in its scope it pervades the entire range of vidyā, both higher and lower. The construction 'taught to Aṅgiras' from the prior clause is to be supplied here as well.
MD_C01_S01_V03: The great householder Śaunaka, having approached Aṅgiras with due ceremony, asked: 'O Bhagavan, what is that, which being known, all this becomes known?' (3)
MD_C01_S01_V03::block-0:
Śaunaka — the descendant of Śunaka — was a mahāśāla, that is, a great householder. To Aṅgiras, the disciple of Bhāradvāja, the ācārya, he approached vidhivat — according to the prescription of śāstra; having so approached, he questioned. From the relation of disciple and teacher between Śaunaka and Aṅgiras, and from the absence of the qualification 'vidhivat' in the prior accounts, it is to be understood that for the earlier sages there was no such formal rule of upasadana. The qualifying word 'vidhivat' is added either to set a limit, or to serve, in the manner of the central‑lamp principle (madhyadīpikā‑nyāya), in both directions — for upasadana is enjoined for us as well as for the prior teachers.

What then did he ask? — 'Kasmin nu bhagavo vijñāte...' Here 'nu' indicates conjecture and reflection; 'bhagavaḥ' is the vocative, 'O bhagavan'; 'all this' — that which is to be known, 'vijñātam' — distinctly cognised. Having heard from the wise the saying 'when the One is known, the knower of all is the knower,' Śaunaka, desirous of ascertaining the particular nature of that One, questioned, asking 'kasmin?' — in what?

Or else, he asked having in his mind the common worldly observation: in the world there are seen many divisions of gold articles — bracelets, rings and the rest — yet by the single knowledge of goldness as one substance they are known to people; just so, must there not be one cause of the entire diversity of the jagat, which being known, all is known? Now an objection: while it is yet unknown whether such a thing exists, the question 'in what?' is improper; the proper question would be 'is there such a thing?' For only when its existence is established can the question 'in what?' arise — as in 'in what should it be deposited?' We answer: not so. From dread of multiplying syllables, and to avoid trouble, the very question 'kim nu asti tat' is intelligently combined into 'kasmin'.
MD_C01_S01_V04: To him he said: Two vidyās are to be known — so indeed the knowers of Brahman declare — namely, the parā and the aparā. (4)
MD_C01_S01_V04::block-0:
To him, that Śaunaka, that Aṅgiras indeed (ha kila) said. What did he say? — 'dve vidye veditavye' — two vidyās, two knowledges, are to be known. So indeed, it is reported, the brahmavids — those who know the meaning of the Veda, the seers of the supreme truth — declare. Which two? He continues: parā, the knowledge of the Paramātman; and aparā, that which has dharma and adharma as its means, and their fruits as its content.

Now there is an objection: Śaunaka had asked, 'in what being known, all is known?' — when that ought to have been answered, Aṅgiras introduces what was not asked, namely 'two vidyās'. This is no fault, for the answer requires a sequence. The aparā is verily an avidyā — that is, it is to be set aside; for so long as the field of avidyā is unknown, nothing is truly known. The nyāya is well established: 'having first refuted the pūrvapakṣa, the siddhānta is to be propounded.' Hence the master here first names the aparā so that, the inferior having been rejected, the supreme may stand revealed.
MD_C01_S01_V05: Of these, the aparā is — the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda, śikṣā, kalpa, vyākaraṇa, nirukta, chandas and jyotiṣa. Now the parā is that whereby the Imperishable is attained. (5)
MD_C01_S01_V05::block-0:
What then is the aparā? It is the four Vedas — Ṛk, Yajus, Sāman, Atharvan — together with the six aṅgas: śikṣā, kalpa, vyākaraṇa, nirukta, chandas and jyotiṣa. This collection has been called aparā vidyā. Now, atha, the parā vidyā is being declared: that whereby the akṣara — to be qualified by what follows — is reached, attained. The verb adhi‑gam is generally taken in the sense of 'reaching', 'attaining'. Nor is there any difference between 'attaining the Supreme' and 'understanding It', for the attainment of the Supreme is nothing other than the cessation of avidyā — it is no further or different thing.

Objection: if the parā vidyā is something other than the Ṛgveda and the rest, how can it then be a vidyā at all, and how can it be the means of mokṣa? For Smṛti declares: 'whatever smṛtis are outside the Veda and whatever heretical views' (Manu 12.95) — from such heretical condition (kudṛṣṭitva) it would be fruitless and inadmissible. Moreover, on this view the Upaniṣads themselves would be outside the Ṛgveda and the rest. And if they are within the Ṛgveda, then to mention 'now the parā' separately is pointless. We answer: not so. The intended sense here is the jñāna which has the akṣara — knowable by the Upaniṣads — as its viṣaya. Here it is the cognition pertaining to that akṣara that is principally meant by parā vidyā, not the body of upaniṣadic words. By the term 'Veda' it is everywhere the body of words that is meant.

Moreover, even after the body of words has been gained, the attainment of the akṣara does not come about without a separate effort — namely, approach to the guru and the rest, and the practice of vairāgya. Therefore brahmavidyā has been distinguished by the words 'now the parā' as something separate. The mere reading of words yields the aparā; but the actual cognition of the imperishable, born of upasadana and detachment, is the parā.
MD_C01_S01_V06: That which cannot be seen, cannot be grasped, has no lineage, no varṇa, no eye nor ear, no hand nor foot — the eternal, the all‑pervading, the omnipresent, the most subtle, the imperishable — that the wise behold as the womb of all beings. (6)
MD_C01_S01_V06::block-0:
In the field of vidhi (injunctive ritual), there is a deed to be performed — agnihotra and the like — at a time other than the cognition of the meaning of the sentence, by gathering up many kārakas such as the agent and so forth. Not so here in the parā vidyā: it is consummated at the very moment the vākyārtha is cognised, since here there is nothing apart from abiding in the cognition of the meaning revealed solely by the word. Therefore the parā vidyā is now distinguished by qualifying its object, akṣara, with the epithets — 'that which is adṛśya', and the rest. Compressing all that is to be said into the buddhi, the text refers to it as if already established by 'yat tat'.

Adṛśya — invisible, that is, beyond the reach of all the buddhīndriyas; for sight, since it operates externally, has the five senses for its instrument. Agrāhya — not the object of the karmendriyas. Agotra — gotra, anvaya, mūla are synonyms; agotra is anantam, that which has no sequence of origin; for it has no source from which it might be derived. Avarṇa — varṇas are the dharmas of dravya, gross qualities like coarseness or shades of white; the akṣara is varṇa‑less, devoid of these.

Acakṣuḥśrotram — eye and ear, the instruments by which beings cognise nāma and rūpa; these are absent in It. From the fact that It is to be qualified as 'omniscient' (Mu.U. 1.1.9), one might suppose, as in saṃsārins, that It accomplishes its purposes through eye, ear and the rest as instruments. That is here negated by 'acakṣuḥśrotram', for the Śruti says, 'eyeless, He sees; earless, He hears' (Śv.U. 3.19). Further, It is apāṇipādam — devoid of the karmendriyas. Being thus ungraspable and ungrasping, It is therefore nityam, indestructible. Vibhum — manifold in form, taking the diverse modes from Brahmā down to the immobile beings. Sarvagatam — all‑pervading, like ākāśa. Susūkṣmam — most subtle, since It is devoid of the gross causes such as sound; for sound and the rest are the successive causes of the grossness of ākāśa, vāyu and so on; lacking these, It is exceedingly subtle.

Furthermore, It is avyayam — by virtue of these very dharmas, it does not waste away. The diminution of one's own limbs, as in the body, is impossible for the limbless. The diminution of treasure, as in the case of a king, is also impossible. Nor is there any diminution by way of guṇa, since It is without guṇa and is the very Self of all. Such a one — the womb of bhūtas, the cause of beings just as the earth is of the sthāvarajaṅgama — that all‑pervading, all‑self, akṣara is beheld (paripaśyanti) by the dhīras, the discerning. The total purport: that vidyā by which such an akṣara is attained is the parā vidyā.
MD_C01_S01_V07: As the spider sends forth and gathers in [its threads], as the herbs spring forth on the earth, as from a living person hairs and bodily down arise — so from the akṣara does this universe come forth. (7)
MD_C01_S01_V07::block-0: It has been said that the akṣara is the bhūta‑yoni. How then is It the bhūta‑yoni? This is now declared by means of dṛṣṭāntas. As, in everyday experience, the well‑known ūrṇanābhi — the spider, the lūtā‑insect — without recourse to any other cause, of itself sends forth threads not different from its own body, projecting them outward; and again gathers in those very threads, drawing them back into its own being. As, on the earth, the herbs — paddy and the rest, the immobile vegetable life — arise, springing forth not as different from the earth itself. As from a sat — that is, from a living conscious puruṣa — hairs (keśa) and the down of the body (loma) come forth, though dissimilar in nature. As these dṛṣṭāntas show, both alike and unlike, so from the akṣara — possessed of the lakṣaṇa already declared, requiring no other instrumental cause — there issues here, in this circle of saṃsāra, the viśva, the entire jagat. The piling up of several illustrations is for ease of comprehension.
MD_C01_S01_V08: By tapas Brahman is augmented; thence is born food. From food, prāṇa, mind, satya, the worlds, and in works the imperishable (fruit). (1.1.8)
MD_C01_S01_V08::block-0:
What evolves out of Brahman — namely this entire universe — comes forth in this fixed sequence and not all at once like a fistful of jujube-fruits flung down together. To declare this regulated order (krama-niyama) the present mantra is begun. By tapas (here glossed by Śaṅkara as jñāna, knowledge — specifically the knowledge of the procedure of creation) the imperishable Brahman, which has just been declared the womb of beings (bhūta-yoni akṣara), cīyate, is, as it were, augmented and swells with the impulse to bring forth this world, just as a seed swells into a sprout, or as a father swells with joy at the birth of a son. The 'tapas' here is therefore not bodily austerity but Brahman's own omniscient knowing of what is to be done.

From that Brahman, thus augmented through the power of omniscience and through the cognition of His capacity for srṣṭi, sthiti and saṁhāra, anna is born. 'Anna' — that which is eaten, enjoyed — denotes here the unmanifest (avyākṛta), the common cause of all transmigrating beings (sarva-saṁsāriṇāṁ sādhāraṇaṁ kāraṇam), now moving into the condition of being about-to-be-differentiated (vyācikīrṣitāvasthā). It is so called because it is destined to become the object of all enjoyment.

From that 'food', i.e. from the avyākṛta in its about-to-be-manifested state, is born prāṇa — Hiraṇyagarbha, who is presided over by Brahman's powers of jñāna and kriyā, who is the common (sādhāraṇa) substratum of the universe, the seed-sprout of the aggregate of avidyā, kāma, karma and the bhūtas, the very Self of the cosmos (jagad-ātmā). The verb 'is born' is to be supplied (anuṣaṅga) here and in what follows.

From that prāṇa, manas — the inner organ characterised by saṁkalpa, vikalpa, saṁśaya and nirṇaya — is born. From that manas, made up of saṁkalpa and the rest, is born satya, here the term for the five mahābhūtas beginning with ākāśa. From these five elements, by the well-known stages of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa-krama), proceed the seven worlds beginning with bhūḥ. In those worlds, by the order of the species men, etc., and by the order of the four varṇas and four āśramas, arise the karmas. And in karmas — the operative causes — resides amṛta, namely the fruit born of those karmas. As long as the karmas are not destroyed even by hundreds of crores of kalpas, so long their fruit is not destroyed: hence it is called amṛta.

Note how Śaṅkara takes 'amṛtam' here strictly in the relative sense — long-lasting karma-phala, not absolute mokṣa. This sets up the contrast that the next section will exploit: ritual fruit is amṛta only relatively; pravṛtti-karma cannot yield the truly imperishable, which is reached only by parā vidyā.
MD_C01_S01_V09: He who is sarvajña, sarvavid, whose tapas is constituted of knowledge — from Him is born this Brahman (Hiraṇyagarbha), name, form and food. (1.1.9)
MD_C01_S01_V09::block-0:
Wishing to gather up and conclude the very meaning that has been stated, and at the same time anticipating what is to follow, this mantra speaks. 'Yaḥ' — He of the qualities just declared, the one named akṣara. 'Sarvajñaḥ' — He who knows everything in general (sāmānyena sarvaṁ jānātīti). 'Sarvavit' — He who knows everything in its particularity (viśeṣeṇa sarvaṁ vettīti). Śaṅkara is careful here to preserve the samāsa-vigraha: omniscience operates at two registers — the universal grasp and the particular grasp — and Brahman possesses both.

Whose 'jñāna-mayam tapaḥ' — that is, whose tapas is itself a transformation of knowledge (jñāna-vikāram eva), having omniscience as its very mark, and devoid of all toil (anāyāsa-lakṣaṇam). Mark well: Śaṅkara explicitly defines this 'tapas' as effortless and consisting of knowledge alone, refuting the Mīmāṃsaka and ritualist supposition that any 'tapas' attributable to the cause of the world must be a form of action or austerity.

From such an omniscient One, this — the kārya-brahman called Hiraṇyagarbha, whose origination has just been described — is born. Further, 'nāma' — proper names such as 'Devadatta', 'Yajñadatta'; 'rūpa' — visible forms such as 'this is white', 'this is blue'; and 'anna' — the eatable substances such as paddy, barley and the rest — all these are born from Him in the order set forth in the previous mantra. There is therefore no contradiction (avirodho draṣṭavyaḥ) between the two mantras: the present one summarises and the previous one detailed.
MD_C01_S02_V01: This is that truth: the works which the seers beheld in the mantras — they are spread out in many ways within the triad (of Vedas). Practise them constantly, you who long for truth: this is your path to the world of well-wrought (karma). (1.2.1)
MD_C01_S02_V01::block-0:
The Vedas-with-aṅgas have already been declared to be the aparā vidyā by the words 'Ṛgvedo Yajurvedaḥ' (Mu.U. 1.1.5) and the rest. The akṣara, whose characteristics were set forth from 'yat tad adreśyam' (1.1.6) down to 'nāma rūpam annaṁ ca jāyate' (1.1.9), is that which is to be reached by parā vidyā: this parā has thus been described together with its viśeṣaṇas. From here onwards, then, the spheres of these two vidyās — saṁsāra and mokṣa — must be discriminated. To do precisely this, the following text is begun.

There, the sphere of the aparā vidyā is saṁsāra, characterised by the difference of agent, instrument, action and fruit (kartṛ-ādi-sādhana-kriyā-phala-bheda-rūpa). It is anādi (beginningless) and ananta (without natural end), being of the nature of duḥkha. It is to be abandoned (hātavyaḥ). For each embodied being individually, and for the totality of beings collectively, it is bound up like an unbroken river-current. The sphere of the parā vidyā is mokṣa: the cessation of that very saṁsāra — anādi, ananta, ajara, amara, amṛta, abhaya, śuddha, prasanna, having one's own Self as its sole resting place, supreme bliss, advaya. Note Śaṅkara's piling up of negations and positives: liberation is not a product but the standing-still of the Self in the Self.

First, then, the sphere of the aparā vidyā is begun with, in order to display its content. For only when its content is displayed does the disenchantment with it (tan-nirveda) become possible. Thus the same śruti will say: 'parīkṣya lokān karma-citān...' (1.2.12). For where there is no display, no examination is possible. Hence, displaying it, the śruti says: 'tat etat satyam' — that is real (avitatham, non-false within its own register). What is real? The 'karmas' such as agnihotra and the rest, declared in the mantras called Ṛgveda etc., illumined by the mantras themselves, which the kavis — the wise sages, Vasiṣṭha and the rest — beheld (apaśyan).

This is 'satya' here in the sense that, within its own province, it is the means to the limited puruṣārtha (svarga). And those Veda-enjoined, ṛṣi-seen karmas are 'tretāyāṁ' — that is to say, in the threefold conjunction of hotra, ādhvarya and audgātra, which is the substratum of the Veda's three-fold employment. Or alternatively, 'in the Tretā age', when ritual was largely current. They are 'bahudhā santatāni' — spread out in many ways, performed continuously by the karmins. Therefore: 'ācaratha' — perform them, 'niyataṁ' — constantly, 'satyakāmāḥ santaḥ' — being desirers of the corresponding karma-fruit just as it really is.

'Eṣa vaḥ panthāḥ' — this is your path; 'sukṛtasya loke' — for the loka, that is, the karma-phala. The 'loka' is so called because what is fruit of one's own performed karma is 'lokyate', is seen and enjoyed there. The sense is: this — namely the agnihotra and the rest enjoined in the trayī — is the path, the unfailing means, for the attainment of that fruit.

One must read this passage carefully. Śaṅkara is not endorsing karma as the supreme path; he is laying out the pūrvapakṣa register of the Veda's own karmakāṇḍa — exactly so that the next mantras can lead the saṁsārin from that to vairāgya. The 'satyakāmāḥ' is precisely those who still seek finite fruit; the true mumukṣu will, by 1.2.12, see through it.
MD_C01_S02_V02: When the flame flickers in the well-kindled fire bearing the oblation, then between the two ājya-portions let him cast the offerings. (1.2.2)
MD_C01_S02_V02::block-0:
There, agnihotra itself is described first by way of illustration, since it has primacy among all karmas. How, then? Just at the moment when, by the placed-in fuel, the hav­ya-vāhana (fire) is well kindled (samiddhe, dīpte), the flame flickers (lelāyate, calati). At that very time, when the flame is dancing on the fire, between the two ājya portions — that is, in the middle, the place of the āvāpa — he should cast (prati­pādayet, prakṣipet) the offerings, with the deity in mind. Because the rite involves the application of multiple-day procedures, the plural 'āhutīḥ' is used.

This — the proper casting of the oblations and the rest — is precisely the karma-mārga, the path leading to the loka (svarga). But its right performance is hard (duṣkaram); and the slips and lapses (vipattayaḥ) are many. Note how Śaṅkara, even while expounding the karma-procedure, is already preparing the listener for the verses that follow: ritual, however prescribed, is intricate, fragile, and easy to spoil. This 'duṣkaram' is the seed of vairāgya.
MD_C01_S02_V03: He whose agnihotra is without darśa, without paurṇamāsa, without cāturmāsya, without āgrayaṇa, without (the rite for) guests, unoffered, without vaiśvadeva, or offered against rule — that very (agnihotra) destroys his seven worlds. (1.2.3)
MD_C01_S02_V03::block-0:
How? 'Whose agnihotra is adarśam' — devoid of the karma called darśa. Because for an agnihotrin the darśa rite is unconditionally obligatory, the fact that 'his agnihotra' is adarśa effectively becomes a description of the agnihotrin himself: that is to say, his darśa is not being performed at all. The same logic applies in 'apaurṇamāsam' and the rest: each is to be understood as a viśeṣaṇa of the agnihotra, since each is its un­distinguishing aṅga.

Apaurṇamāsam — devoid of paurṇamāsa-karma. Acāturmāsyam — devoid of cāturmāsya-karma. Anāgrayaṇam — āgrayaṇa is to be done in autumn etc.; he in whom that is not done. Atithivarjitam ca — the daily honouring of guests is not done by him. Ahutam — properly offered at agnihotra time, it is not duly offered by his own hand. Just like adarśa etc., avaiśvadevam — devoid of vaiśvadeva-karma. And avidhinā hutam — even when offered, it is offered improperly, contrary to the rule (ayathāhutam).

Thus laden with defects, ill-accomplished or unaccomplished, what does this so-called agnihotra do? — it is told: 'āsaptamān' — up to and including the seventh — 'tasya lokān hinasti' — destroys the worlds of that performer. 'Hinasti' here is virtually 'as good as destroys', because he obtains nothing but mere toil (āyāsa-mātra-phalatvāt). When karmas are well performed, in proportion to the maturation of the karma, the seven worlds beginning with bhūḥ and ending in satya are won as fruit. Those worlds, when not won by an agnihotra of the kind just described, are 'as it were destroyed' — for the toil is undeniable, but the fruit fails. Hence 'hinasti' is used.

Alternatively, those connected through the favour of piṇḍa-dāna and the like — pitṛ, pitāmaha, prapitāmaha and putra, pautra, prapautra, that is, those seven who confer benefit on one's own self (sva-ātma-upakārāḥ sapta lokāḥ) — they too do not come about by such defective agnihotra; hence again 'hinasti' (he destroys) is the verb. Note how the śruti deliberately escalates: not merely fruitlessness, but positive injury to ancestors and progeny. This is the karma-kāṇḍa's own warning of how easily the path collapses — preparing the ground for the renunciate counsel of the next mantras.
MD_C01_S02_V04: Kālī, Karālī, Manojavā, Sulohitā, Sudhūmravarṇā, Sphuliṅginī, and Viśvarucī — these seven flickering tongues are of the deity (Fire). (1.2.4)
MD_C01_S02_V04::block-0: Kālī, Karālī, and Manojavā, and Sulohitā, and she who is Sudhūmravarṇā; Sphuliṅginī, and Viśvarucī — these are the goddess(es), flickering, the tongues of the burner. From Kālī down to Viśvarucī, these flickering ones are the seven tongues of Agni, whose function is to swallow up the oblations cast as havis. The naming is meant for upāsanā within the karma-paddhati: the sādhaka, when offering, is to know each tongue by its name, so that the oblation is, as it were, consciously consigned. This too is part of the discipline whose intricacy was indicated above.
MD_C01_S02_V05: He who, in these (tongues) shining bright, performs (his rites) at the proper times, him these — the oblations, becoming the rays of the sun — lead to where the one Lord of the gods has his abode. (1.2.5)
MD_C01_S02_V05::block-0:
In these — the differentiated tongues of fire — he who, the agnihotrin, 'carate' — performs the karma, agnihotra and the rest, in those bright (bhrājamāneṣu, dīpyamāneṣu) tongues; and 'yathā-kālam' — that is, without transgressing the time appointed for each particular karma; the offerings, taking the yajamāna, lead him. These oblations — the very ones performed by him — having become the rays of the sun (sūryasya raśmayaḥ bhūtvā), that is, by way of those rays, lead him 'where' — to that svarga in which the lord of the gods, Indra, the one (eka) who dwells over all (sarvān upari adhi-vasati), is the adhivāsa, the indweller.

Observe what Śaṅkara is quietly doing: the deva-yāna here is firmly attached to ritual punctuality. The 'yathā-kālam' is essential — the same act offered out of season is the deficient agnihotra of 1.2.3. Even the highest ritual reward is hedged about with conditions of time, place, agent, and rule. Compare this with the unconditioned reach of parā-vidyā, which knows no kāla.
MD_C01_S02_V06: Saying 'Come, come!' the bright-shining oblations bear the yajamāna by the rays of the sun, addressing pleasing words and worshipping him, (saying:) 'This is your puṇya, well-wrought brahma-loka.' (1.2.6)
MD_C01_S02_V06::block-0:
How do they bear the yajamāna by the rays of the sun? It is told: 'Ehi, ehi!' — calling him thus, the oblations bear that yajamāna; and they are 'suvarcasaḥ' — luminous, dīptimatyaḥ. Further, 'priyām vācaṁ abhivadantyaḥ' — uttering pleasing speech of the form of stuti and the rest; and 'arcayantyaḥ' — worshipping him; (saying) 'eṣaḥ vaḥ' — this is yours — 'puṇyaḥ sukṛtaḥ brahma-lokaḥ', the fruit. Thus uttering pleasing speech, they bear him. Here 'brahma-loka' means svarga only, by force of the prakaraṇa.

Note Śaṅkara's careful gloss 'brahma-lokaḥ svargaḥ prakaraṇāt': in the present context of karma-mārga, the phrase brahma-loka must not be confused with the supreme abode of parā-vidyā — it is merely the highest svarga reached by deva-yāna. The śruti is still wholly within the aparā register, displaying its very best fruit. Even this best, however, is reached only by being addressed, flattered and welcomed by one's own oblations: the soul of the karmin is praised, but it is praised within saṁsāra. The next mantras will, by contrast, dismantle this very glamour.
MD_C01_S02_V07: Verily, these eighteen sacrificial forms — in which the inferior karma is enjoined — are unsteady rafts; the deluded who hail this as the highest good go again and again to old age and death.
MD_C01_S02_V07::block-0:
This karma — bereft of knowledge, yielding only this much fruit, the very effect of avidyā, kāma, and karma — is therefore unsubstantial and the root of suffering, and so is here censured. "Plavāḥ" means perishable, that is, given to ruin. "Hi" — for, since these are "adṛḍhāḥ," unstable; "yajña-rūpāḥ" means yajña-nirvartakāḥ, the very forms by which the sacrifice is accomplished — eighteen in number, namely the sixteen ṛtviks together with the wife and the yajamāna, making eighteen.

Resting upon these eighteen, the karma — that is, the karma which is avara, merely karma divorced from knowledge — is what scripture has spoken of. Hence, since these eighteen, being the substrata of inferior karma, are themselves unstable and so float away, the karma resting on them floats away too, along with its fruit; just as when the pot is destroyed, the milk, curd, and the like that stand within it perish along with it. Since this is so, those undiscriminating fools who rejoice in this karma — "etat śreyaḥ" — taking it to be the means to the highest good, having dwelt in svarga for a little while, again and verily go to old age and death (jarā-mṛtyu).
MD_C01_S02_V08: Dwelling within avidyā, fancying themselves wise and learned, the deluded wander about, struck again and again — like blind men led by one who is himself blind.
MD_C01_S02_V08::block-0: Further: dwelling "in the midst of avidyā" — that is, in its very interior — being given to non-discrimination, fancying themselves "we ourselves are dhīrāḥ — possessed of intellect, paṇḍitas, those who have known what is to be known" — esteeming their own ātman in this fashion, and being "jaṅghanyamānāḥ" — being struck and severely afflicted by the throngs of countless ills such as old age and disease — these mūḍhas wander about (pariyanti), bewildered. Because they are bereft of vision (darśana-varjitatvāt), they are "led by the blind" — led by one himself eyeless, by one whose path is being shown to them by such a guide. As in the world the blind, deprived of sight, fall into pits and upon thorns, just so are these.
MD_C01_S02_V09: Dwelling in avidyā in manifold ways, the childish imagine "we have accomplished our purpose"; since these karmins, on account of attachment, do not truly know the Truth, they, struck down by sorrow, fall from their world when their merit is exhausted.
MD_C01_S02_V09::block-0: Further: "avidyāyāṃ bahudhā" — dwelling in avidyā in manifold ways, in many forms — "we ourselves are kṛtārthāḥ" — those who have accomplished what was to be done, who have fulfilled their purpose — thus do the bālas, the ignorant, conceit themselves and harbour pride. Because ("yat" = yasmāt) the karmins, being thus, "do not truly know" — do not know the tattva — owing to rāga, that is, owing to being overpowered by attachment to the fruit of karma; for that reason, becoming "āturāḥ," stricken with sorrow, and being "kṣīṇa-lokāḥ," those whose karmic-fruits are spent, they fall away (cyavante) from svarga-loka.
MD_C01_S02_V10: Holding sacrifice (iṣṭa) and works of public utility (pūrta) to be the highest, the utterly deluded know no other good. Having enjoyed their merit upon the summit of svarga, they enter again this world, or one yet lower.
MD_C01_S02_V10::block-0:
"Iṣṭāpūrtam" — "iṣṭa" being the śrauta karma such as the yāgas, and "pūrta" being the smārta works such as wells, ponds, water-tanks and the like — esteeming this very thing as par excellence the means of puruṣārtha, holding it to be "variṣṭha," foremost, they do not know the other (anyat), namely the means to śreyas which goes by the name of ātma-jñāna; they do not know it, these "pramūḍhāḥ," deluded by their distractedness over sons, cattle, kinsfolk, and the like.

And they, upon the "pṛṣṭha" of "nāka," the upper region of svarga — in that abode of enjoyment which is their sukṛta-fruit — having experienced the fruit of karma, again enter this world (imaṃ lokam), the human world, or one even lower (hīna-tara) than this — characterised by tiryaks, narakas and the like — according to the residue of their karma.
MD_C01_S02_V11: But those who, dwelling in the forest, practise tapas and śraddhā — those calmed sages who, knowing, live by alms — they go through the door of the sun, freed of stain, to that abode where dwells the immortal Puruṣa, of imperishable nature.
MD_C01_S02_V11::block-0:
But others, who are endowed with the knowledge contrary to the foregoing — vānaprasthas and saṃnyāsins — "tapaḥ-śraddhe" — "tapaḥ" being the karma enjoined for their respective āśrama, and "śraddhā" being the vidyā having Hiraṇyagarbha and the like as its object — they "upavasanti," serve, these tapas and śraddhā while dwelling in the forest. "Śāntāḥ" — those whose troop of organs has been quieted. "Vidvāṃsaḥ" — and the householders who are predominantly given to knowledge: that is the meaning. "Bhaikṣa-caryāṃ carantaḥ" — practising the life of mendicancy; since they are without possessions, they dwell in the forest — such is the connexion.

"Sūrya-dvāreṇa" — by the northern path indicated by the sun — they, becoming "virajāḥ" — virajasaḥ, those whose puṇya-pāpa-karmas are exhausted — "prayānti," go forth in eminence to where, in the Satyaloka and the like, the immortal Puruṣa, the prathamaja Hiraṇyagarbha, is the "avyaya-ātmā" — of imperishable nature, abiding so long as saṃsāra abides. Thus far indeed extend the courses of saṃsāra accessible to aparā-vidyā.

Now, do some hold this to be mokṣa? No. Because of śrutis like "ihaiva sarve pravilīyanti kāmāḥ" (Mu.U. 3.2.2) and "te sarvagaṃ sarvataḥ prāpya dhīrā yuktātmānaḥ sarvam evāviśanti" (Mu.U. 3.2.5); and because of the prakaraṇa — for in a passage that has set out to describe aparā-vidyā there can be no sudden intrusion of the topic of mokṣa. The "viraja"-state here is only relative (āpekṣika). The whole effect of aparā-vidyā, characterised by sādhya and sādhana, the duality marked off by the divisions of kriyā, kāraka, and phala — this dvaita extends only thus far, ending in the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha. So too has Manu spoken, while enumerating the saṃsāric courses beginning with the immobile: "Brahmā, the Viśva-sṛjas, Dharma, the Mahat, and the Avyakta — these the wise call the highest sāttvic course" (Manu 12.50).
MD_C01_S02_V12: Having examined the worlds heaped up by karma, let the brāhmaṇa come to dispassion: "the uncreated cannot be reached by the created." To know That, let him, samit in hand, approach a guru — a śrotriya, established in Brahman.
MD_C01_S02_V12::block-0:
Now, however, in order to display the eligibility, in regard to parā-vidyā, of him who is wholly disenchanted with the entire saṃsāra of the form of sādhya-sādhana, this is set forth — "parīkṣya." Whatsoever is the domain of the aparā-vidyā beginning with the Ṛgveda — to be performed by a man burdened with the natural defects of avidyā, kāma, and karma, since it has been enjoined for that very man who is yet possessed of the defects of avidyā etc.; whatsoever the worlds, the fruits, that are the effect of such performance — those marked off as the Southern and Northern paths — and whatsoever fruits, marked by hells, beasts and pretas, are produced by the defect of non-performance of the enjoined and transgression of the prohibited:

having examined all these, ascertaining their true nature in every way through pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, and āgama; the worlds — the saṃsāric courses ranging from the unmanifest down to the immobile, marked by the vyākṛta and avyākṛta, mutually causing one another's birth like seed and sprout, crowded with hundreds of thousands of evils unnumbered, sapless as the core of a plantain-stem, like to māyā, mirage-water, gandharva-cities, dream, foam, and bubbles, perishing every instant — having turned all these to one's back; "karma-citān" — heaped up by karmas set in motion by the defects of vidyā and kāma — that is, fashioned by dharma and adharma; this is the meaning.

"Brāhmaṇaḥ" — the brāhmaṇa is taken specifically because his alone is the privileged eligibility, by total renunciation, for brahma-vidyā: such is the import of the word "brāhmaṇa." "Having examined the worlds, what should he do?" — that is now stated: "nirvedam." "Vid" with "nis" prefixed is here in the sense of vairāgya; let him "āyāt" — attain — vairāgya. The mode of that vairāgya is shown thus: in this saṃsāra there is not a single thing that is uncreated (akṛta). For all the worlds whatsoever are heaped up by karma, and being made by karma they are non-eternal. The implication is — there is nothing eternal whatsoever. All things, however, are but the means of the non-eternal. For all karma is fourfold in its work — utpādya (to be produced), āpya (to be attained), vikārya (to be modified), or saṃskārya (to be refined); beyond this there is no domain of karma.

And I have need of the eternal, the immortal, the fearless, the kūṭastha, the immovable, the ever-firm reality — not of its opposite. What then is to be gained by karma, abundant in toil, the very means of anartha? Becoming thus disenchanted, in order to know — to attain by way of distinction — that which is the fearless, auspicious, uncreated, eternal padam, he, that disenchanted brāhmaṇa, should approach the guru, the ācārya endowed with śama, dama, and the rest. The force of the emphatic "the guru alone" (gurum eva) is to teach that even one learned in śāstra should not undertake the search for brahma-jñāna independently.

"Samit-pāṇiḥ" — bearing in his hand a bundle of fuel — he should approach a "śrotriya" — one who through study has heard out and become possessed of the meaning of the texts — and a "brahma-niṣṭha," that is, one who has set aside all karmas and whose niṣṭhā is in Brahman alone, the non-dual; just as one says "japa-niṣṭha" or "tapo-niṣṭha." For there can be no brahma-niṣṭhatā in a karmin, since karma and ātma-jñāna stand in mutual contradiction. Having approached that guru after the prescribed manner and having pleased him, he should ask him concerning the akṣara, the Puruṣa, the satyam.
MD_C01_S02_V13: To him who has approached, whose mind is fully calmed, who is endowed with self-restraint — to such a one the wise teacher imparted, in its very essence, that brahma-vidyā by which one knows the akṣara, the Puruṣa, the satyam.
MD_C01_S02_V13::block-0:
To him: that vidvān, the guru, the brahma-vit, to the upasanna — to him who has approached. "Samyak" — that is, in accordance with śāstra. "Praśānta-cittāya" — to one whose defects of pride and the like have been quieted. "Śamānvitāya" — to one endowed also with cessation of the outer senses, that is, to one wholly dispassionate.

By what jñāna, by what supreme vidyā, one knows that very akṣara — qualified as adṛśya etc., that very akṣara designated by the word "puruṣa" because of fullness (pūrṇatvāt) and because of lying (śayanāt) within the city (puri); the satyam — that very [akṣara], avyaya by reason of being its own paramārtha-svabhāva; and akṣara — by reason of non-flowing-away (akṣaraṇāt), inexhaustibility, and unwastable nature — that brahma-vidyā the guru "prokta," he taught — "prabrūyāt" is the sense — "tattvataḥ," exactly as it is.

And this same is the niyama for the ācārya too: that he must rescue from the great ocean of avidyā the worthy disciple who has come to him by the legitimate way.
MD_C02_S01_INTRO1::block-0: The whole effect of aparā-vidyā has been spoken of. And this saṃsāra — that whose sāra it is, that very root from which it arises and into which it again merges — that akṣara, called "Puruṣa," the satyam, is the topic of the parā brahma-vidyā: that on whose being known all this here becomes known. He is to be set forth — and so the subsequent text is now begun:
MD_C02_S01_V01: That [Brahman] is this Truth: as from a well-kindled fire countless sparks of like nature spring forth, even so, O dear one, manifold beings are born from the Imperishable (akṣara), and into That alone do they return.
MD_C02_S01_V01::block-0:
That truth which falls within the scope of the apara-vidyā, characterized as the fruit of action, is only relative truth. But the truth here intended is the object of the parā-vidyā, since it is marked by the supreme reality (paramārtha-sat). "That is this truth" — that is, what is real in itself, the object of true knowledge (vidyā); the other, being the object of avidyā, is unreal (anṛta).

Since the akṣara is utterly remote from sense-perception, the question naturally arises: how then can men ever apprehend the imperishable as truth, in the manner of something perceptible? To meet this, the śruti gives an illustration. "As from a well-kindled fire (sudīptāt pāvakāt) — that is, from fire that is thoroughly blazing and inflamed — sparks (visphuliṅgāḥ), particles of fire, issue forth in thousands, of identical nature with the fire itself (sarūpāḥ)." Even so, from the akṣara of the character described above, manifold beings (vividhāḥ bhāvāḥ) — that is, jīvas — come into being. They are "manifold" because they conform to the differences of the various bodily upādhis. O dear one (saumya), just as the spaces enclosed within pots and the like, though in themselves not different from ākāśa, appear as different cavities by reason of the differences of pots and other limiting adjuncts, so do these jīvas appear in conformity with the manifold upādhis fashioned by name and form.

Thus they are born following upon the rise of the bodily upādhis fashioned by various names and forms; and "into that alone" — into that very same akṣara — "they return" (apiyanti), dissolving in conformity with the dissolution of the bodily upādhis, just as the cavities within pots dissolve when the pots are broken. As ākāśa's apparent role as the cause of the origin and dissolution of the cavities is wholly due to the upādhis of pot and the like, even so the akṣara's seeming causality with respect to the origin and dissolution of jīvas is due solely to the bodily upādhis fashioned by name and form.
MD_C02_S01_V02: Divine, formless is the Puruṣa, with outer and inner alike, unborn, without prāṇa, without manas, pure, higher than the highest Imperishable.
MD_C02_S01_V02::block-0:
Higher than the akṣara that is called the unmanifest (avyākṛta) — which is the seed of all name and form, and is itself called "akṣara" only relatively, namely with reference to its own modifications — there stands That which is the very own form of the imperishable, free from every distinction wrought by upādhi, like ākāśa devoid of every shape, to be set forth by such characterizations as "not this, not this" (neti neti). Wishing to declare this, the śruti says — "divine" (divyaḥ): possessed of self-luminosity (dyotanavān), since He shines by His own light. Or "divya" means "abiding in the heaven of His own Self," or "transcendent of the world."

"Hi" ("for") — because He is formless (amūrtaḥ), free from every shape; "puruṣa" — full (pūrṇa), or that which lies in the citadel (puriśaya); "with outer and inner alike" (sabāhyābhyantaraḥ) — that is, He abides together with the outer and the inner. "Unborn" (ajaḥ) — He is not born from anything, since neither birth in itself nor a cause of birth exists for Him. As wind and the like are causes for water-bubbles, or as the pot and the like are causes for the apparent cavities in ākāśa, so for Him no such cause exists. Since all the modifications of being have birth as their root, by negating birth all the rest are negated. "With outer and inner alike, He is unborn" — therefore He is undecaying, immortal, imperishable, eternal, and fearless: this is the meaning.

Though, by reason of the various views which take their stand upon the differences of bodily upādhis, He appears as if endowed with prāṇa, manas, the senses, and their objects — just as ākāśa appears tarnished with mire and the like — yet, in His own self-nature, in the view of those who behold the supreme reality, He is "without prāṇa" (aprāṇaḥ): the air which is the principle of motion, with its various powers of action, is non-existent in Him, and so He is aprāṇa. Similarly, "without manas" (amanāḥ): the manas, which is endowed with various powers of cognition and which is of the nature of saṅkalpa and the rest, is also non-existent in Him; hence He is amanāḥ. By the words "aprāṇaḥ" and "amanāḥ" should be understood the negation of the various forms of vital air such as prāṇa, the organs of action and their objects, as well as the buddhi, the manas, the organs of knowledge, and their objects — as in another śruti, "He, as it were, meditates; He, as it were, vibrates" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7).

Since thus both pairs of upādhis are negated in Him, He is "pure" (śubhraḥ), stainless. Therefore He is "higher than the akṣara" (akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ) — than that akṣara, namely the unmanifest (avyākṛta), which has been characterized as marked by the upādhi of being the seed of name and form, and which, since it is observed as the seed of all effects and instruments, is itself indicated as the higher principle relative to its modifications. Beyond that akṣara, the unconditioned Puruṣa is "para" — this is the meaning. In Him, that ākāśa-named akṣara, the field of all empirical dealings, is woven warp-and-woof.

But how is His being free of prāṇa and the rest established? It is replied: if prāṇa and the rest existed in their own essence prior to their origination, just as the Puruṣa exists in His own essence, then indeed the Puruṣa might be said to be "endowed with prāṇa" because of the existence of prāṇa and the rest in Him. But prāṇa and the rest do not exist prior to their origination. Hence the supreme Puruṣa is "endowed with prāṇa" only in a figurative sense — just as Devadatta is called "sonless" so long as no son has been born to him.
MD_C02_S01_V03: From Him are born prāṇa, manas, and all the sense-organs; ākāśa, vāyu, fire, the waters, and earth that supports all.
MD_C02_S01_V03::block-0:
How is it, then, that prāṇa and the rest do not exist [prior to creation]? It is replied: "From Him" — from this very Puruṣa marked by the upādhi of being the seed of name and form — "is born" prāṇa, which is the object of avidyā, a modification, a mere designation, of the nature of the unreal. As another śruti declares, "The modification is only a name, having its origin in speech; clay alone is the truth" (Chā. Up. 6.1.4); and elsewhere it is called "unreal" (anṛta). The supreme Self cannot be "endowed with prāṇa" through that prāṇa which is the object of avidyā and is unreal — just as a man without a son cannot become a father by means of a son seen in dream.

In the same way, "manas, all the sense-organs," and their objects — these too are born from Him alone. Therefore it is established that He is, without any figurative attribution, free from prāṇa and the rest: this is the meaning. And as they are non-existent in their own essence prior to origination, even so they should be regarded as non-existent at dissolution.

As the inner instruments — manas and the senses — are thus described, so are the elements which serve as the substratum of the body and its objects: "kham" — ākāśa; "vāyu" — the outer wind in its divisions of āvaha and the rest; "jyoti" — fire; "āpaḥ" — water; "pṛthivī" — the earth, the supporter of all (viśvasya dhāriṇī). These elements, having for their successive qualities sound, touch, colour, taste, and smell — each later one carrying with it the qualities of the preceding ones — are all born from Him alone.
MD_C02_S01_V04: Fire is His head; the moon and the sun are His two eyes; the quarters are His ears; the revealed Vedas are His speech; the wind is His prāṇa; the universe is His heart; from His feet was born the earth — He, indeed, is the inner Self of all beings.
MD_C02_S01_V04::block-0:
Having declared in brief, in the mantra beginning "divyo hyamūrtaḥ" (Mu. Up. 2.1.2), the imperishable Puruṣa — without distinction, the truth that is the object of the parā-vidyā — the śruti now sets out to expound that very same Puruṣa once more in expanded form, with distinctions. For when an object is taught both in brief and in detail, it is easily grasped, as in the relation of sūtra and bhāṣya.

Now, it might seem that the Virāṭ — the cosmic person within the egg, who is born from the firstborn prāṇa, that is, from Hiraṇyagarbha — though appearing as a tattva mediated by another tattva, is nevertheless born from this very same Puruṣa and is constituted of Him. To establish this, the śruti now describes Him in detail. "Agniḥ" — the heaven-world, as another śruti says, "That world, O Gautama, is fire" (Chā. Up. 5.4.1). "Mūrdhā" — that of which fire is the highest limb, the head; "cakṣuṣī" — the moon and the sun are His two eyes. The relative pronoun "yasya" ("of whom") is to be supplied throughout, by transposing the demonstrative "asya" ("of this") into "yasya."

"Diśaḥ śrotre" — of whom the quarters are the two ears; "vāgvivṛtāś ca vedāḥ" — of whom the famous, revealed (uncovered) Vedas are the speech; "vāyuḥ prāṇaḥ" — of whom the wind is the prāṇa; "hṛdayam" — the inner instrument; "viśvam" — the entire universe — is of this one. For all this universe is nothing but a modification of the inner instrument, since in deep sleep the dissolution of the world is observed within manas alone, and even in waking it is from manas alone that things spread out, like sparks from fire. "Yasya ca padbhyāṃ jātā pṛthivī" — He from whose feet earth was born — this divine Viṣṇu, the infinite, the first embodied one, having the three worlds for His bodily upādhi, is the inner Self of all beings (sarvabhūtāntarātmā). For He, in all beings, is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower, the very self of all instruments.
MD_C02_S01_V05: From Him is fire, of which the sun is the kindling-stick; from soma comes Parjanya; the herbs grow upon the earth; the male sheds seed in the female — many are the offspring brought forth from the Puruṣa.
MD_C02_S01_V05::block-0: And those creatures who transmigrate by the path of the five sacrificial fires — they too are declared to come into being from that very Puruṣa.
MD_C02_S01_V05::block-1: From that supreme Puruṣa arises the fire that is the special form of the abode of the offspring. This is further specified — "of which the sun is the kindling-stick (samidhaḥ)": the sun functions as the fuel-stick, for by the sun the heaven-world is kindled. From that, namely from the heaven-fire thus brought into being, comes Parjanya — the second fire — through Soma. From that Parjanya, the herbs (oṣadhayaḥ) grow upon the earth. The herbs, when offered as oblation in the man-fire and serving as the material cause, become the seed; then the male, the man-fire (puruṣāgni), "sheds seed in the female (yoṣitāyām)" — that is, in the woman who is the woman-fire. Thus, in this sequence, "many offspring" (bahvīḥ prajāḥ) — Brāhmaṇas and the rest — are "brought forth from the Puruṣa" (puruṣāt samprasūtāḥ), arising from that supreme Puruṣa.
MD_C02_S01_V06: From Him come the Ṛk-mantras, the Sāman, the Yajus, the consecrations, all sacrifices, the soma-rites, the dakṣiṇās, the year, the sacrificer, and the worlds in which the moon purifies and the sun shines.
MD_C02_S01_V06::block-0:
Furthermore, the means of action and their fruits also come from Him alone. How? "From the Puruṣa" come the Ṛk-mantras (ṛcaḥ), namely the mantras with fixed syllables, fixed feet, and fixed cadence, distinguished by the gāyatrī and other metres; the Sāman, having the fivefold and the sevenfold subdivision, distinguished by the stobha and the modes of chant; the Yajus — sentences of unfixed syllables, unfixed feet, and unfixed cadence. Thus the mantras are of three kinds.

"Dīkṣāḥ" — consecrations marked by the muñja-girdle and the rest, the various rules concerning the agent. "Yajñāś ca sarve" — all sacrifices: the agnihotra and the rest. "Kratavaḥ" — those that involve the sacrificial post (yūpa). "Dakṣiṇāś ca" — sacrificial fees, beginning with a single cow and ending with the gift of one's entire wealth. "Saṃvatsaraḥ" — time, which is an auxiliary of the sacrificial act. "Yajamānaḥ" — the agent. "Lokāḥ" — the worlds that are the fruit of his action. These worlds are specified — "yatra somaḥ pavate" — those worlds in which the moon purifies the worlds; and "yatra sūryaḥ" — those in which the sun shines. These two are reached by the southern and northern paths respectively, and are the fruits, the one of the unwise agent, the other of the wise agent.
MD_C02_S01_V07: From Him also come, in manifold ways, the gods, the sādhyas, men, beasts, and birds, prāṇa and apāna, rice and barley, austerity, faith, truth, brahmacarya, and rule.
MD_C02_S01_V07::block-0: And from that Puruṣa, the gods who are members of the sacrificial action come forth in manifold ways (bahudhā), through the various groups — the Vasus and the rest — "sam-prasūtāḥ" — fully brought forth. The sādhyas — a particular class of gods; men — those qualified for action; cattle — domestic and wild; birds — the fowl. The life-breath of men and the rest, namely prāṇa and apāna; rice and barley, which serve as oblational substances; austerity (tapas) — both as an auxiliary of action, of the nature of inner refinement, and as an independent means of fruit; faith (śraddhā) — that mental clarity, that conviction of belief, which precedes the application of every means of human aim; likewise truth (satyam) — the avoidance of falsehood and the speaking of what accords with the fact, and that which causes no injury; brahmacarya — abstention from sexual intercourse; and rule (vidhi) — the prescription of "how-it-is-to-be-done."
MD_C02_S01_V08: Seven prāṇas spring from Him, seven flames, seven kindling-sticks, seven oblations, these seven worlds in which the prāṇas move — placed in the cave, seven and seven [in each living being].
MD_C02_S01_V08::block-0:
Furthermore, the seven prāṇas — the prāṇas of the head — arise from that very same Puruṣa. Of these there are seven flames (sapta arciṣaḥ), the lights, the illuminations of their respective objects. Likewise seven kindling-sticks (samidhaḥ): the seven objects, for the prāṇas are kindled by their objects. Seven oblations (sapta homāḥ): the cognitions of those objects — as another śruti says, "That which is His knowledge, that He pours forth as oblation" (Tai. Nār. 80).

Furthermore, "these seven worlds" (sapta ime lokāḥ) — the seats of the senses — "in which the prāṇas move" (yeṣu caranti prāṇāḥ); "prāṇāḥ" is here qualified by "caranti" — "in which the prāṇas move" — and this qualifier serves to set aside prāṇa, apāna, and the rest. "Guhāśayāḥ" — those that lie in the cave, that is, in the body or in the heart, since they sleep there during sleep. "Nihitāḥ" — placed by the Ordainer, "sapta sapta" — seven and seven, in the case of every living being. Both the actions of the wise (those who sacrifice in the Self), together with their fruits; and the actions of the unwise, together with their means and fruits — all this comes forth from that supreme, all-knowing Puruṣa: such is the purport of this section.
MD_C02_S01_V09: From this Puruṣa, all oceans and mountains arise; from this flow forth the rivers of every form. From this come all herbs and the sap, by which, encompassed by the elements, the inner self truly stands.
MD_C02_S01_V09::block-0:
From this — that is, from that very Puruṣa — arise all the oceans, the salt-ocean and the rest. The mountains too, the Himavat and the others, all proceed from this very Puruṣa. From this they flow forth, that is, they stream out — the rivers, the Gaṅgā and the rest, called sindhus, of every form, of manifold shapes. From this very Puruṣa likewise come all the oṣadhis, the herbs such as rice and barley. The rasa too — the sixfold sap of sweet and the other tastes — issues from him; for it is by this rasa, when one is encompassed (pariveṣṭita) by the five gross elements, that the inner self abides — that is, the antarātman, namely the liṅga-śarīra, the subtle body, truly stands. And thus is the etymology brought out: because that subtle body, lying in the interval (antarāle) between the gross body and the [supreme] Self, conducts itself as though it were the self, it is called antarātman — "the inner self."

Thus is shown how, from the one Puruṣa, the entire world of waters, mountains, rivers, plants, sap and the embodied subtle self proceeds, by which the chain of cause and effect in saṃsāra is sustained — the very chain that the parā-vidyā teaches one to transcend.
MD_C02_S01_V10: The Puruṣa alone is all this — work, austerity, and the supreme immortal Brahman. He who knows this, set in the cave [of the heart], O dear one, here itself rends asunder the knot of avidyā.
MD_C02_S01_V10::block-0:
Thus, from the Puruṣa is this entire world born forth. Therefore, on the principle declared elsewhere — "All modification is mere name, originating in speech; the Puruṣa alone is the truth" — vācārambhaṇa, the modification, the name-giving, is unreal, while the Puruṣa alone is satya. Hence "Puruṣa eva idaṃ viśvam" — the Puruṣa alone is this entire universe; there is nothing whatever named "viśva" apart from the Puruṣa.

Thus what was promised in the opening — "Knowing what, O Bhagavan, is all this known?" (Mu.U. 1.1.3) — is here being answered. For when this supreme Self, the Puruṣa, the cause of all, is known, then it stands known that "the Puruṣa alone is this universe; there is nothing else" — and so all is known.

Now, what then is this "viśva"? It is described thus: karma — that whose mark is the agnihotra and the other rites; tapas — knowledge, [or austerity], whose fruit is otherwise constituted; this whole universe is, in its first aspect, the effect of these. And these themselves are the effect of Brahman. Therefore the entire universe is Brahman, the parām amṛtam, the supreme deathless. "I myself am that" — he who knows it thus, set (nihitaṃ sthitam) in the cave, that is, in the heart of all living beings — he, by such knowledge, rends asunder the avidyā-granthi, the knot, that is, the deeply hardened latent impressions of avidyā taking the form of a knot. Vikirati — he scatters, disperses, destroys [it] here itself, while still living, not after death — O Saumya, O dear-faced one.

Thus the bhāṣya teaches jīvanmukti: liberation arises from knowledge alone, here in this very life; the knot of avidyā that binds saṃsāra is loosened by parā-vidyā, not by any quantum of karma or tapas, since karma and tapas themselves are merely effects within the causal field of Brahman.
MD_C02_S02_V01: Manifest, well-established, moving in the cave by name, the great seat — in this is all this lodged: that which moves, breathes, blinks, and which does not — know that, the existent and non-existent, the most desired, beyond cognition, that which is greatest among living beings.
MD_C02_S02_V01::block-0:
Since the akṣara, being formless, is hard to apprehend, the manner of its knowing is now expounded.

Āviḥ — manifest in light. Saṃnihitam — well-established, that is, near at hand through the upādhis of speech and the rest; for, by another śruti, "It blazes, it shines" — it appears as though apprehending word and the rest. By the dharmas of the upādhis — seeing, hearing, deliberating, knowing, and so on — having become as it were manifest, it is marked out in the heart of every living being. This Brahman that has thus become manifest, set well (saṃyak sthitam) in the heart, is called "guhā-cara" by name — "that which moves in the cave"; for, since it shows itself through the modes of seeing, hearing and the rest, it is renowned as "guhā-caram." Mahat — great, on account of being greater than all. Padam — that which is reached (padyate) by all, since it is the resort of all things-meant.

How, then, is it the "great seat"? It is said: because here, in this Brahman, etat sarvam — all this — is samarpitam, made entirely to enter, like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel. Ejat — that which moves, the bird-tribe and the rest; prāṇat — that which breathes, that is, men, beasts and so on, possessed of prāṇa, apāna and the rest; nimiṣat — that which has the activity of blinking and the like; and from the word "ca" we are to take in also that which does not blink. All this, in its entirety, is here itself, in Brahman, lodged.

This seat (āspada) of all — "jānatha" — know, O disciples, recognising it as none other than your own Self. Sat-asat — having the nature of being and non-being, that is, of the embodied (mūrta) and the unembodied (amūrta), of the gross and the subtle; for nothing exists apart from these two. Vareṇyam — to be chosen; for, on account of its eternity, it alone is to be sought by all. Param — beyond, that is, beyond cognition (vijñānāt prajānām); the syntactical link is that it is beyond the empirical knowledge of beings, that is, not within the range of laukika-vijñāna. Yat variṣṭham — most excellent, the very best among all things-meant that count as choicest; for that one Brahman, being free from every defect, is supremely the best.

The school that takes "sat" alone or "asat" alone as ultimate is hereby refuted: Brahman, while in itself nirupādhika, is the substratum of both the embodied and unembodied orders, and therefore is termed "sad-asat"; not, however, in the sense of being literally a thing-among-things — for it is param, transcending the cognising apparatus by which gross and subtle alike are apprehended.
MD_C02_S02_V02: That which is luminous, smaller than the smallest, in which the worlds are lodged together with their dwellers — this is that imperishable Brahman; it is prāṇa, it is speech and mind. This is the truth, this is the immortal — that, O dear one, is to be pierced; pierce it.
MD_C02_S02_V02::block-0:
Further: yat arcimat — that which is luminous, possessed of dīpti; for by its dīpti the sun and the rest shine — hence Brahman is dīptimat. Further: yat aṇubhyaḥ — than the very smallest such as the śyāmāka grain — aṇu ca — even more subtle; and from the word "ca" we are to understand that, beyond the gross too, beyond earth and the rest, it is exceedingly gross.

In which the worlds — bhūr and the rest — are nihitāḥ, lodged; and lokinaḥ — those who dwell in the worlds, men and the rest, who are seats of consciousness, as is well known. This very thing, the substratum of all — akṣaraṃ brahma — that is the imperishable Brahman; saḥ prāṇaḥ — it is the prāṇa; tat u vāṅmanaḥ — it is speech, it is mind, and all the karaṇas; tat u — it is the inner caitanya. For the entire aggregate of prāṇa, the senses and the rest, has consciousness as its substratum, as said in the other śruti: "the prāṇa of prāṇa" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.10).

That inner caitanya which is the akṣara of prāṇas and the rest — this is satya, the unfailing; therefore, amṛta, indestructible. Tat veddhavyaṃ — that is to be pierced by the mind; that is, in it the mind is to be made one-pointedly fixed (samādhāna) — that is the meaning. Since it is so, O Saumya — viddhi — fix the mind firmly upon the akṣara.

Note how Śaṅkara explicates the word "veddhavya": piercing here is not literal but is the inward concentration (samādhāna) by which the mind is fixed in the akṣara — a clear contrast between the pravṛtti-mode of outward action and the nivṛtti-mode of inward absorption proper to the renunciate.
MD_C02_S02_V03: Taking up as bow the great weapon of the Upaniṣads, one should fix on it an arrow whetted by upāsanā; drawing it back with a mind absorbed in That, O dear one, pierce that very imperishable as the target.
MD_C02_S02_V03::block-0:
How is it to be pierced? It is said: dhanuḥ — the bow, the iṣv-āsana, gṛhītvā, having taken up; aupaniṣadam — that which has its being in the Upaniṣads, well known there; mahāstram — and that great weapon, namely the bow great in itself; in that, [fix] a śara, an arrow.

What sort of arrow? It is upāsā-niśitam — sharpened, that is, attenuated and refined by the continuous abhidhyāna of upāsanā — saṃskṛta, that is its meaning. Sandadhīta — one should perform the sandhāna, the joining. And, having joined, āyamya — drawing back, that is, withdrawing the antaḥkaraṇa together with the indriyas from their own objects, and turning them solely toward the target — this is the import; for here the drawing back is not, as with a bow, possible by the hand alone.

Tadbhāvagatena cetasā — by a mind that has gone forth to the bhāva, the contemplation, of that Brahman, the akṣara, the target. Lakṣyaṃ tadeva — that very target with the characteristics already declared — akṣaram, O Saumya, viddhi — pierce.

Thus the bhāṣya makes explicit the inward turn (pratyak-pravṛtti) demanded by the renunciate path: the drawing of the bow stands for the indriya-saṃyama by which the antaḥkaraṇa, withdrawn from objects, is poured wholly into the akṣara.
MD_C02_S02_V04: The praṇava is the bow; the arrow is verily the Self; Brahman is said to be the target. By the unwavering it is to be pierced; one should become identified with That, like the arrow.
MD_C02_S02_V04::block-0:
What was spoken of as bow and the rest is now expounded.

Praṇavaḥ — the oṃ-kāra — is the bow. Just as the iṣv-āsana is the cause of the arrow's entering the target, so the oṃ-kāra is the cause of the ātman-arrow's entering the target which is the akṣara. For, by the praṇava that is being repeated, [the seeker] becomes purified (saṃskriyamāṇa) and, taking it as ālambana, comes to rest in the akṣara without obstruction — just as an arrow that has been shot from a bow comes to rest in the target. Hence the praṇava is bow-like — "dhanuḥ."

Śaro hyātmā — the arrow is the ātman, characterised by upādhis, who is none other than the Supreme — entered into the body, like the sun and the rest reflected in water, as witness of all the buddhi-pratyayas. He, like an arrow lodged in his very own self, is to be lodged in the akṣara-Brahman; therefore Brahman is said to be tat lakṣyam — "that target," since for those wishing to enter samādhi the mind takes hold of it in the manner of a target, regarding it under the form of one's own Self.

This being so, apramattena — by one free of the carelessness of thirst for outer objects, completely dispassionate, with senses subdued, with single-pointed mind — Brahman, the target, is to be pierced. After such piercing, śaravat tan-mayaḥ bhavet — like the arrow, one should become identified with That. As the arrow's becoming one-natured with the target is its fruit, so by the dispelling of the conceit "I am the body" and the rest, one should bring about the fruit of being one-natured with the akṣara — this is the meaning.

Note the precise import: the "ātman" that is here the arrow is not the supreme Self in its absolute aspect but the upādhi-bound jīva — the witness in the body — which, recognising its identity with the akṣara, is dissolved into it. The piercing is therefore the final undoing of adhyāsa, by which the upādhi-conditioned self is restored to its true aupaniṣadika-svarūpa.
MD_C02_S02_V05: In whom heaven, earth and the mid-region are interwoven, together with mind and all the prāṇas — know him alone as the one Self; let go all other words. This is the bridge to the immortal.
MD_C02_S02_V05::block-0:
Because the akṣara is hard to indicate, repeating the statement is for the sake of clear indication.

Yasmin — in which akṣara, in the Puruṣa — dyauḥ, pṛthivī, ca antarikṣaṃ — heaven, earth and the mid-region; and manas with the prāṇas, that is, with all the other karaṇas — otaṃ — interwoven, samarpitam, made wholly to enter. Tameva — that very one, the substratum of all, ekaṃ — one without a second; jānatha — know, O disciples — ātmānam — as the inmost Self (pratyak-svarūpa) of yourselves and of all living beings.

And having known him, anyāḥ vācaḥ — other words, of the form of apara-vidyā — vimuñcatha — let go, abandon. And likewise, all the karma together with its instruments which is to be illumined by them. For — "amṛtasya eṣa setuḥ" — this knowledge of the Self is, as it were, a bridge for the attainment of the immortal, of immortality, of mokṣa; it is the cause of crossing the great ocean of saṃsāra. So says the other śruti: "Knowing him alone, one passes beyond death; there is no other path for the going [to liberation]" (Śv.U. 3.8).

Observe the explicit contrast Śaṅkara draws here: aparā-vidyā — comprising the karma-kāṇḍa and its prescriptive vāk — is to be relinquished by the renunciate who has found his footing in parā-vidyā. The bridge metaphor is read tightly: it is not karma but ātma-jñāna alone that bridges the saṃsāra-ocean; "nānyaḥ panthāḥ" rules out every other path for liberation.
MD_C02_S02_V06: Where the channels are gathered together like spokes in a chariot-hub, there, within, this Self moves about, taking birth manifoldly. Meditate on the Self as Oṃ; may it be well with you for the crossing beyond darkness.
MD_C02_S02_V06::block-0:
Further: arā iva — just as spokes are made to enter into the hub of a chariot, even so saṃhatāḥ — gathered together, made to enter — yatra — in which heart, [are] the nāḍīs that pervade the body in every direction; in that very heart, as witness of the buddhi-pratyayas, saḥ eṣaḥ — this very Self that is the topic — antaḥ — within, in the middle — carate — moves, abides; seeing, hearing, deliberating, knowing, bahudhā — in many ways, as if being born again and again through the pratyayas of anger, joy and the rest, on account of conforming to the antaḥkaraṇa-upādhi. For ordinary people say: "He is born glad," "he is born angry."

That very Self — "oṃ-iti evam" — taking the oṃ-kāra as ālambana, by the imaging declared above, dhyāyatha — meditate, reflect upon. Both what was to be told has been told, and the disciples, on account of their wish to know the Brahma-vidyā, have ceased from karma and have entered upon the path to liberation. For their unobstructed attainment of Brahman the ācārya pronounces a benediction: svasti — let it be well with you, that is, without obstruction. Pārāya — for [reaching] the further shore. Of what? — Of avidyā-tamas, the darkness of avidyā; that is, for the going to one's own true Brahma-self, free of avidyā — this is the meaning.

Mark the structure here: the disciples have already become nivṛtta-karman through the rise of vividiṣā, and the upadeśa is completed by an āśīrvāda from the teacher. The benediction is itself in the nivṛtti register — not for the gain of any worldly prosperity, but for the safe traversal beyond the darkness of avidyā into the avidyā-rahita-brahma-svarūpa. This is the closing note proper to the Sringeri lineage's rendering of the parā-vidyā teaching: jñāna alone, supported by oṃ-kāra-upāsanā, is the means; mokṣa is the unobstructed reaching of one's own ever-present Self.
MD_C02_S02_V07: He who is omniscient and all-knowing — His is this glory upon the earth. In the divine city of Brahman, in the ether (within the heart), this Self is established.
MD_C02_S02_V07::block-0:
That which, beyond darkness, is to be reached only after crossing the great ocean of saṁsāra — the object of parā-vidyā — in what does it abide? To this the śruti replies: He who is sarvajña (omniscient as to the totality) and sarvavit (knowing every particular), as already explained. He is further specified — yasya eṣa mahimā: whose is this well-known glory, this all-pervading lordly power.

And what is that mahimā? It is this: by whose government heaven and earth stand upheld in their stations; by whose command sun and moon revolve unceasingly like a whirling firebrand; by whose ordinance rivers and oceans do not transgress their bounds; by whose rule the moving and the unmoving are held to their course; by whose decree the seasons, the two ayanas, and the years do not overstep their order; and by whose ordinance agents, their actions, and the fruits thereof do not depart from their proper times. This is His mahimā — His upon the earth, in the worlds. Such a god is sarvajña, of such majesty.

‘In the divine (divye) city of Brahman’ — divine, i.e. luminous, since it is the place where every cognition of the intellect (bauddha-pratyaya) shines forth, brahmapure, the city of Brahman. For here Brahman, in its very nature as caitanya (pure consciousness), is eternally manifest. The ‘city of Brahman’ is the lotus of the heart; the vyoman within it is the ākāśa lodged in the cavity of that heart-lotus, and there the Self is, as it were (iva), established (pratiṣṭhitaḥ). For in one who, like ākāśa, is all-pervading, going, coming, or fixed location cannot otherwise be made out — these are spoken of only by upādhi.
MD_C02_S02_V08: Of the form of mind, the leader of the prāṇa and the body, established in food, having lodged the heart (the buddhi within the heart-lotus) — Him do the wise behold, all-pervadingly, by special knowledge: the immortal of the form of bliss, which shines forth.
MD_C02_S02_V08::block-0:
That Self, dwelling there (in the heart-lotus), is grasped only through the modifications of the mind (manas-vṛttis); hence ‘manomaya’ — so called because manas serves as His upādhi, not because He is in Himself constituted of mind. ‘Prāṇaśarīra-netā’ — the prāṇa and the body that go with it form the prāṇaśarīra; He is the leader (netā) of that aggregate, drawing it forth from this gross body towards another, subtle body.

‘Pratiṣṭhitaḥ anne’ — established in food: that is, in the bodily lump that is the transformation of the food daily consumed, daily growing and decaying. ‘Hṛdayaṁ saṁnidhāya’ — having placed the heart, i.e. the buddhi, in the cavity of the lotus of the heart. For the Self’s station is precisely this lodging in the heart; the Self does not in truth have a station in food. Food is named only as the locus of the body, while the heart (buddhi) is the locus of His direct manifestation.

That tattva of the Self — ‘tad’ — the dhīras, the men of viveka, ‘paripaśyanti’: they behold it as full on every side; not by ordinary cognition, but by viśiṣṭa-vijñāna — by knowledge specially generated through the teaching of śāstra and ācārya, and ripened by śama, dama, dhyāna, total renunciation (sarva-tyāga), and vairāgya. They behold it as ānanda-rūpa — of the form of bliss, freed from every anartha, duḥkha, and exertion, sukha-rūpa; as amṛta — immortal; ‘yad vibhāti’ — which shines forth specially, ever in one’s own Self alone.
MD_C02_S02_V09: The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder, and his karmas are exhausted, when That is seen — That which is both the higher and the lower.
MD_C02_S02_V09::block-0:
Now the fruit of this knowledge of the supreme Self is being declared. ‘Hṛdayagranthi’ — the knot of the heart, namely desire (kāma), constituted of the latent impressions of avidyā and lodged in the buddhi as its support, as another śruti has it: ‘the desires which lie hid in his heart’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.7; Kaṭha 2.3.14). It is heart-lodged (hṛdayāśraya), not Self-lodged (nātmāśraya); for the Self is in itself unattached. ‘Bhidyate’ — it is split, that is, it goes to destruction.

‘Chidyante sarva-saṁśayāḥ’ — all doubts concerning every knowable object, doubts that, for ordinary men, run on like the current of the Gaṅgā until death, are cut off and brought to a halt. To one whose doubts have thus been severed and whose avidyā has ceased — for him, those karmas wrought before the rise of jñāna in this birth and in former births, whose fruit has not yet begun, together with those which arise concomitantly with the rise of jñāna, are exhausted (kṣīyante). But not those karmas which have already initiated this present body: these, having begun their fruition (pravṛtta-phala), must be exhausted by enjoyment.

‘Tasmin parāvare dṛṣṭe’ — when That, the all-knower, the trans-saṁsāric, the parāvara — para in His aspect as cause, avara in His aspect as effect — that very parāvara is seen directly as ‘I am He’, then, the root cause of saṁsāra being uprooted, one is liberated. This is the import.
MD_C02_S02_V10: In the supreme golden sheath dwells Brahman, taintless and partless. That is pure, the Light of lights, That which the knowers of the Self know.
MD_C02_S02_V10::block-0:
The three subsequent mantras give a concise statement of the very theme already set forth. ‘Hiraṇmaye’ — luminous, of the splendour of light, namely the radiance of buddhi-vijñāna; ‘pare kośe’ — in the supreme sheath, ‘kośa iva aseḥ’ — like the scabbard of a sword.
