It is termed ‘para’, supreme, because it is the locus of the realisation of the Self’s own nature, and because it is innermost to all (sarvābhyantaratvāt).

There abides ‘virajam brahma’ — Brahman free from the dust-stain of avidyā and all its allied defects (rajo-mala). It is ‘niṣkalam’ — partless: as ‘sarva-mahattva’ and ‘sarvātmaka’, it is partless in the sense that no kalās, no parts or limbs, depart from it; that is, niravayava. Because it is virajam and niṣkalam, it is, therefore, ‘śubhram’ — pure; and ‘jyotiṣāṁ jyotiḥ’ — the illuminator of all luminaries such as fire and so forth, all of which are themselves of the nature of light.

The sense is: even fire and the rest are luminous only by reason of the indwelling Brahman-Self caitanya-jyotis. That, indeed, is the supreme jyotis which is illumined by no other and which is itself self-luminous Self-light. ‘Tad ātma-vido viduḥ’ — that the knowers of the Self, who, as men of viveka, know the Self — their own Self, the witness of every cognition concerning sound and the rest of the sense-objects — they alone know That; the followers of the inward pratyaya (ātma-pratyaya-anusāriṇaḥ) know it, not those who follow the pratyaya of outward objects. Since it is the supreme jyotis, those alone know it, none other.
MD_C02_S02_V11: There the sun does not shine, nor moon nor stars; nor do these lightnings shine — much less this fire. Him alone, as He shines, all things shine after; by His radiance all this shines forth.
MD_C02_S02_V11::block-0:
How is That ‘the Light of lights’? It is now told. ‘Na tatra’ — there, in That very Brahman which is one’s own Self, even the sun, otherwise the illuminator of all, does not shine; the meaning is, the sun does not illumine that Brahman. For the sun illumines all that is non-Self only by His (Brahman’s) radiance; the sun has no power of illumination of itself. Likewise the moon and the stars, likewise these lightnings, do not shine there. ‘Kuto’yam agniḥ’ — how then this fire which falls within our perception?

Why multiply instances? Whatever in the universe shines, all that, in shining, only shines after Him — that supreme Lord — who, being self-luminous (svato-bhārūpatvāt), is Himself shining (bhāntam): they kindle from Him, follow His shining. Just as water, or a firebrand and the like, when joined with fire, burns along with the burning fire, not of its own power — so by His radiance alone, by His effulgence, all this — sun and the rest — shines forth.

Since it is thus, that very Brahman both ‘shines’ (bhāti) and ‘shines forth’ (vibhāti) — the latter through the manifold radiance present in its effects. Hence its very nature as bhā-rūpa, light-natured, is established of itself. For what is itself non-luminous cannot bestow illumination on another: pots and the like are not seen to illumine other things, while the sun and the like, themselves of the form of light, are so seen.
MD_C02_S02_V12: Brahman alone is this Immortal in front; Brahman behind, Brahman to the south and to the north, below and above; pervading everywhere, Brahman alone is this universe, the supreme.
MD_C02_S02_V12::block-0:
‘That which is the Light of lights, Brahman — That alone is real (satya); all is its modification, “a transformation in name only, taking its rise in speech” (vācārambhaṇaṁ vikāro nāmadheya-mātram), the rest is unreal’ — this very theme, having been established at length and with reasoning, is now drawn to a close, in the manner of an upasaṁhāra mantra.

‘Brahmaiva’ — Brahman alone, of the character already defined — ‘this’ which, in front, appears, to those of avidyā-vision, as if it were not Brahman; just so, behind, Brahman; just so, to the south; just so, to the north; just so, below; just so, above. On every side, as though something other than itself, it has spread forth in the form of effects, manifesting as endowed with name and form (nāmarūpavad-avabhāsamānam).

Why multiply words? ‘Brahmaiva idaṁ viśvaṁ’ — Brahman alone is this entire universe; ‘variṣṭham’ — most excellent, most pre-eminent. The cognition of non-Brahman, in every form, is mere avidyā — like the cognition of a serpent in a rope. ‘Brahman alone is the one paramārtha-satya’ — this is the very teaching of the Veda.
MD_C03_S01_INTRO1::block-0:
Parā-vidyā has been declared — that by which is reached the Akṣara, called Puruṣa, the Real, the satya; on whose attainment there comes the absolute destruction of the heart-knot and the rest, the very causes of saṁsāra. The means of seeing It — yoga — has been set forth by way of the imagery of the bow and the rest (the Praṇava-bow, the Self-arrow, etc.).

Now, accordingly, the auxiliaries of that vidyā — the disciplines of satya and the rest — must be enunciated; for that purpose the subsequent text is begun. And the determination of the Reality, which is paramount, is now carried out by yet another method. Because of the extreme difficulty of fathoming this Truth, even after what has already been done, an introductory mantra of sūtra-character is laid down, with a view to the firm ascertainment of the supreme Reality —
MD_C03_S01_V01: Two birds, ever-united companions, friends, cling to one and the same tree. Of these, one tastes the sweet fruit (the pippala); the other, eating not, looks on.
MD_C03_S01_V01::block-0:
‘Dvā’ — two; ‘suparṇā’ — two suparṇas, ‘śobhana-patanau suparṇau’, of fair flight; or, by the general usage of ‘suparṇa’ for ‘bird’, simply two birds. ‘Sayujā’ — sayujau, ever yoked together; ‘sakhāyā’ — sakhāyau, ‘samāna-ākhyānau’, of one common name, ‘samāna-abhivyakti-kāraṇau’, sharing one and the same cause of manifestation. Such being their case, they have embraced ‘samānam vṛkṣam’ — one same tree — same in being a common substratum of experience — the body, called a ‘tree’ because, like a tree, it is destined to be cut down (uccheda-sāmānyāt). The two have clung round it, ‘pariṣasvajāte’, like two birds round one tree, with a view to the enjoyment of its fruit.

This tree is the well-known one — ‘ūrdhva-mūla, avāk-śākha, aśvattha’ (root above, branches below, the holy fig), springing from the avyakta as its root, designated kṣetra, the support of the karma-fruit of every living being. Round that tree the two ‘suparṇas’ have closed their embrace: namely, the kṣetrajña-jīva, who is the ātman conditioned by the liṅga-upādhi made of avidyā, kāma, karma and vāsanās, and the īśvara, conditioned (as upādhi) by the pure sattva.

Of these two thus clinging, ‘anyaḥ’ — the one, the kṣetrajña, having taken his stand on the liṅga-upādhi tree, ‘pippalam’ — the karma-born fruit characterised as sukha and duḥkha, sweet, that is, of the savour of manifold and varied feelings, ‘atti svādu’ — eats it as something delicious, enjoys it, through avivekatā (want of discrimination). ‘Anaśnan anyaḥ’ — the other, namely Īśvara, of nature eternally pure, awakened, free, the omniscient, conditioned by sattva-upādhi, eats not. He is the prompter of both — bhojya and bhoktṛ, the enjoyed and the enjoyer — through His mere being, by His standing as eternal sākṣin. He, eating not, ‘abhicākaśīti’ — merely sees. For Him, His prompting consists in mere seeing, just as a king’s rule consists in mere presence.
MD_C03_S01_V02: On the same tree, the puruṣa, sunk down and bewildered, grieves on account of his powerlessness; but when he beholds the other—the Lord, who is worshipped (or, who is the dear one)—and His glory, then he becomes free from sorrow.
MD_C03_S01_V02::block-0:
Such being the situation, on the same tree—that is, in the body described above—the puruṣa, the experiencer, the jīva, weighed down by the heavy load of avidyā, desire, action, the fruits thereof, attachment and the rest, sinks down like a gourd in the waters of the ocean: having decisively fallen into the notion that the body itself is the Self, he holds, ‘I alone am this; I am so-and-so’s son, his grandson; lean, stout, virtuous, devoid of virtue, happy, sorrowful’—such is his cognition; ‘there is none other than this body,’ he thinks. He is born, he dies, he is united and disjoined with kin and friends.

Hence, by anīśā—by powerlessness: the wretched state of mind, ‘I am unable to do anything; my son is dead, my wife is dead, what use is life to me?’—such helpless feeling is anīśā—through that he grieves, is consumed; muhyamānaḥ, becoming bewildered through indiscrimination by manifold misfortunes, falling into inner anxiety. Such a one, transmigrating through the wombs of pretas, beasts, men and the rest in the manner of a swing-pendulum (ājavañjavī-bhāva), at some moment, after many births, by reason of merit accumulated through pure dharma, has the path of yoga shown to him by some supremely compassionate teacher; endowed with non-injury, truthfulness, brahmacarya, total renunciation, śama, dama and the rest, with mind composed.

When, at that time, he beholds—meditating—the other: distinct from the locus marked by the limiting adjunct of the tree—juṣṭam, that is, who is resorted to by many through the paths of yoga and by the ritualists; the Īśa, the Lord, the non-transmigrant, transcending hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age and death, the Lord of all the world; ‘I am He; the Self of all, equal in all, present in all beings; not the other, the māyic one, delimited by the upādhis born of avidyā’—and beholds His mahiman, His glory, namely, ‘the universe-form is His, of this Supreme Lord who is none other than myself’—when he sees thus, then he is vītaśokaḥ, freed from sorrow, released from the entire ocean of grief; he becomes one whose work is accomplished (kṛtakṛtya). This is the meaning.
MD_C03_S01_V03: When the seer beholds the puruṣa of golden hue, the Maker, the Lord, the source of Brahmā, then that knower, shaking off both merit and demerit, taintless, attains supreme equality.
MD_C03_S01_V03::block-0: Another mantra states this very same purport with greater elaboration. When—at whatever time—paśyaḥ paśyati: ‘paśyaḥ’ means a knower, a sādhaka; he beholds, as before, the rukmavarṇam, that is, of the very nature of self-luminosity, or whose imperishable light is like that of gold; the Maker of the entire universe; the Īśa, the Lord; the Puruṣa; the Brahma-yoni—either, ‘That which is Brahman and is the source (yoni) is brahma-yoni,’ him; or, ‘the source (yoni) of the inferior brahman’—when he beholds Him in this manner, then that wise seer, having shaken off, cast away, burnt up at the root the bondage-constituting actions, the puṇya-pāpe (merit and demerit), becomes nirañjanaḥ, untainted, his afflictions gone; and he attains the parama, the supreme, unsurpassed sāmya, equality, characterized by non-duality. Equalities pertaining to the realm of duality are all on this side of it (lower than it); hence this, marked by non-duality, is the supreme equality, which he attains, that is, accomplishes.
MD_C03_S01_V04: He, indeed, is Prāṇa, who shines variously through all beings; the wise one, knowing Him, becomes no over-asserter (ativādī). Sporting in the Self, delighting in the Self, performing action—he is the foremost among the knowers of Brahman.
MD_C03_S01_V04::block-0:
Furthermore: He who is the Prāṇa of prāṇa, the Supreme Lord—this very one, the topic under discussion—indeed by all beings, from Brahmā down to the tuft of grass, ‘viviban-shines’: the third case here is in the sense of qualification (ittham-bhūta-lakṣaṇā tṛtīyā). The meaning is: being the Self of all, abiding in all beings, He shines variously, illuminates manifoldly. Such a one—abiding in all beings—he who, knowing Him directly with the awareness ‘I am this,’ that is, the wise one (vidvān): merely by the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, ‘he does not become’—does not become what? An ativādī, ‘over-asserter,’ that is, one whose habit it is to speak, transcending all others. He who knows the Self directly as the Prāṇa of prāṇa is no over-asserter. When all is seen as the Self alone—nothing else exists—what then could he assert as transcending? He who has another, an inferior, seen, asserts that as transcending it. This wise one, however, sees nothing other than the Self; hears nothing other; knows nothing other. Hence he is no over-asserter.

Further: ātma-krīḍaḥ—he whose play, sporting, is in the Self alone and not elsewhere, in son, wife, and the like—he is ātma-krīḍaḥ. Likewise, ātma-ratiḥ—he whose rati, delight, fondness, is in the Self alone—he is ātma-ratiḥ. The distinction is: krīḍā depends upon external means; rati, however, is independent of means and is mere fondness for an external object. So too, kriyāvān: he whose kriyās are jñāna, dhyāna, vairāgya and the like, is the kriyāvān here. In a samāsa reading—‘ātmaratir-eva kriyāsya vidyate’—either the bahuvrīhi or the matup-suffix becomes redundant.

Some, however, wish that this verse establishes the conjoint performance of agnihotra and the rest along with brahma-vidyā (jñāna-karma-samuccaya). But that is contradicted by the principal-meaning words ‘He is the foremost of the knowers of Brahman.’ For one engaged in external action cannot at the same time be ātma-krīḍa and ātma-rati. Only one withdrawn from external activity becomes ātma-krīḍa, since external action and ātma-krīḍā are mutually opposed. Darkness and light cannot exist together in one place at the same time. Therefore, this exposition of jñāna-karma-samuccaya is mere unfounded babble; and so also from the śrutis ‘abandon other speech’ (Mu.U. 2.2.5) and ‘through the yoga of saṃnyāsa’ (Mu.U. 3.2.6). Therefore, the kriyāvān here is precisely he who possesses the kriyās of jñāna, dhyāna and the like—a saṃnyāsin who has not transgressed the limits of the noble (ārya-maryādā). He who, possessed of these characteristics, is no over-asserter, sporting in the Self, delighting in the Self, performing such kriyā, established in Brahman—he is the foremost, the chief, of all knowers of Brahman.
MD_C03_S01_V05: By truth indeed is this Ātman to be attained, by tapas, by right knowledge, by brahmacarya constantly maintained. Within the body, of the nature of light, pure, He is whom the strivers of cleansed faults behold.
MD_C03_S01_V05::block-0:
Now the auxiliary means to right knowledge for the bhikṣu—truth and the rest, predominantly belonging to the path of nivṛtti—are enjoined. He is to be attained by satya, that is, by the abandoning of falsehood, by the abandoning of speaking what is contrary to fact. Further, ‘by tapas indeed’—by the one-pointedness of senses and mind. Because of the smṛti, ‘the supreme tapas is one-pointedness of mind and senses’ (Mokṣa-dharma 250.4). That alone, being conducive to facing the vision of the Self, is the supreme means; tapas, not anything else such as cāndrāyaṇa. ‘This Ātman is to be attained’ is to be supplied throughout. By samyag-jñāna, by the vision of the Self as it really is. By brahmacarya, by abstaining from sexual intercourse. Nityam, ‘constantly,’ always: ‘constantly by truth,’ ‘constantly by tapas,’ ‘constantly by right knowledge’—the word ‘nityam’ is to be construed everywhere by the maxim of antar-dīpikā (the inner-lamp principle). And He will say further, ‘in whom there is no crookedness, no falsehood, no māyā’ (Pra. U. 1.16).

Where is this Ātman who is attained by these means? It is said: ‘antaḥ-śarīre’—within the middle of the body, in the lotus-cavity (puṇḍarīka-ākāśa); jyotir-mayaḥ, of golden hue, śubhraḥ, pure—that Ātman whom yatayaḥ, those of the nature of striving, the saṃnyāsins, of cleansed faults—those whose mental defilements such as anger have been worn down—paśyanti, behold, attain. That Ātman is constantly attained by saṃnyāsins through the means of truth and the rest. He is not attained by occasional truth-telling and the rest. This is an arthavāda whose purpose is the praise of the means of truth and the rest.
MD_C03_S01_V06: Truth alone wins, not falsehood; by truth is laid out the path called devayāna, by which the seers, having attained their desire, ascend to where lies the supreme treasure of truth.
MD_C03_S01_V06::block-0:
Satyam eva—the truthful one alone—jayate, conquers; not the anṛta, not the speaker of untruth—this is the meaning. For there cannot be victory or defeat of mere truth and falsehood unsupported by a person. It is well known in the world that the speaker of untruth is overcome by the speaker of truth, and not the reverse; therefore, the powerful efficacy of truth as a means is established.

Further, the supreme efficacy of truth as a means is also known from śāstra. How? By truth—by the practice of speaking what is in conformity with fact—the path called devayāna is laid out, extended, continuously operative. By that path, indeed, the ṛṣis, the seers, who are free from trickery, māyā, deceit, ego, hypocrisy and falsehood, the āpta-kāmas, those whose thirst has departed in every way—ākramanti, ascend; yatra, where, that paramārtha-tattva, the supreme treasure (nidhāna) belonging to satya as the highest means and as the goal—prakṛṣṭam, supreme—is deposited (ni-dhīyate) in the form of the goal of human life (puruṣārtha), and so is called nidhāna. There by the path along which they ascend—that path is laid out by truth: this is the connection with the foregoing.
MD_C03_S01_V07: Vast and divine, of inconceivable form, subtler than even the subtle, He shines; far beyond the far, He yet stands here near, hidden in the cave for those who see.
MD_C03_S01_V07::block-0: What is It and of what nature?—this is now told. Bṛhat, vast, mahat, is that Brahman under discussion, since by the means of truth and the rest it is pervaded everywhere. Divyam, self-luminous, not within the range of the senses; therefore acintya-rūpam, ‘its form cannot be conceived.’ Subtler than even ākāśa and the rest, since its subtlety is unsurpassed because it is the cause of all; vibhāti, shines variously, that is, shines in various forms—as sun, moon, and the rest. Further, dūrāt, from a far place, sudūre, in a yet farther place, it abides, since for the ignorant the Brahman is utterly inaccessible. Iha, here in this body, antike, near—because for the wise it is the very Self, and because of being the inmost of all (since even ākāśa is heard of as having something inner to it). Iha paśyatsu, ‘here, among those who see,’ that is, among the conscious beings; nihitam, deposited, abiding—observed by the yogins as that which is endowed with the activity of seeing and the like. Where? Guhāyām, in the cave, that is, in the buddhi. There indeed, the wise mark Him, hidden. Even though so abiding, being veiled by avidyā, He is not marked by the unwise, although He stands right there.
MD_C03_S01_V08: He is not seized by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other gods (senses), nor by tapas, nor by karma; but by the clarity of knowledge, when one has become pure of essence—from that, indeed, when meditating, one beholds Him, the partless.
MD_C03_S01_V08::block-0:
Once again, the unique means of Its attainment is told. Since na cakṣuṣā gṛhyate, He is not grasped by the eye by anyone, because of being formless; nāpi vācā, nor by speech, because of not being denotable; na cānyair devaiḥ, nor by the other senses; even though tapas is the means of all attainments, He is not grasped by tapas; so too, although by Vedic karma such as agnihotra, well known for its greatness, He is not grasped.

What then is the means of His grasp? It is said: jñāna-prasādena, ‘by the clarity of knowledge.’ The knowledge of all living beings, though by nature capable of revealing the Self, when polluted by faults such as attachment to external objects, becomes unclear, impure; then, although the Self-reality is ever-present, it does not reveal it, just as a mirror covered with dirt or as agitated water cannot reveal the reflection. When, by the removal of the impurity of attachment and the rest born of the contact of the senses with their objects—as in the case of the mirror or water—it is rendered clear, pure, tranquil, and steady, then jñāna-prasāda comes about. By that clarity of knowledge, viśuddha-sattvaḥ—of cleansed inner organ—he becomes fit to behold Brahman; from that—tatas tu—he beholds, attains, that Self, niṣkalam, free from all distinction of parts, dhyāyamānaḥ, meditating: that is, he, possessed of truth and the rest as means, with the senses withdrawn, with one-pointed mind meditating, contemplating Him.
MD_C03_S01_V09: This Ātman, subtle, is to be known by the cetas (cleansed mind), in whom prāṇa has entered fivefold; by the prāṇas the entire mind of creatures is pervaded; when that mind is purified, this Ātman shines forth.
MD_C03_S01_V09::block-0:
The Self whom one beholds in this manner: eṣaḥ aṇuḥ, subtle, is the Ātman, to be known by the cetas alone, that is, by pure knowledge alone. Where is He? In the body wherein the prāṇa, vāyu, has entered samyak, well, in fivefold form as prāṇa, apāna and the rest—in that very body, in the heart—He is to be known by the mind. This is the meaning.

By what kind of cetas is He to be known? It is said: prāṇaiḥ saha, ‘together with the senses’: the entire antaḥ-karaṇa of all creatures is pervaded by these prāṇas, ‘woven through’ (otam), as milk by butter, as wood by fire. For the antaḥ-karaṇa of all creatures is well known in the world as endued with consciousness. And in whatever cetas is freed from the impurities of kleśa and the rest and is purified, vibhavati—shines forth—there does this aforesaid Ātman shine forth in a special manner, by Himself, that is, He reveals Himself. This is the meaning.
MD_C03_S01_V10: Whatever world he of pure mind clearly envisages in his mind, and whatever objects of desire he longs for — that very world he wins, and those very desires. Therefore one who seeks prosperity should worship the knower of the Self. (10)
MD_C03_S01_V10::block-0:
He who, as set forth above, has cognised the Self of all as his own Self — by reason of that very status of being the Self of all, the result that accrues to him is described as the attainment of all. The text shows it thus: 'whichever world' — be it the world of the fathers and the rest — 'he envisages clearly in the mind' (saṃvibhāti), that is, resolves in his sankalpa, thinking 'let it be mine, or let it be for another'; the qualification 'of pure sattva' (viśuddhasattvaḥ) means one whose afflictions (kleśa) are exhausted, the knower of the Self whose inner organ has become unstained; 'whatever desires (kāmān) he longs for' — whatever enjoyments he prays for; 'that very world he wins' (jayate), that is, attains, 'and those very desires', that is, the enjoyments resolved upon in his thought.

Because the resolves (sankalpa) of such a knower are unfailingly true (satya-sankalpatva), therefore one who seeks prosperity (bhūti-kāmaḥ) — desirous of vibhūti — 'should worship the knower of the Self' (ātma-jñam arcayet), that is, him whose inner organ stands purified by Self-knowledge. The worship is to be done by washing his feet, by service, by salutations and the like. Hence such a one is alone fit to be honoured.
MD_C03_S02_V01: He knows that supreme abode of Brahman, wherein the universe is set and shines pure. The wise who, free from desire, worship the Puruṣa — they pass beyond this seed (of birth). (1)
MD_C03_S02_V01::block-0: Inasmuch as 'he knows' (vedo jānāti) — namely, that knower of the Self whose worship was just enjoined — 'this Brahman of the said description, the supreme abode' (paramaṃ dhāma), the highest substratum (āśraya, āspada) for all desired ends; 'wherein' — in which Brahman, the abode — 'the entire universe is laid down' (nihitam), that is, deposited; and which by its own light shines 'pure' (śubhram), unsullied — therefore that Self-knower, the Puruṣa thus endowed, is to be worshipped like the supreme deity. Those who, being 'free from desire' (akāmāḥ), shorn of the thirst for vibhūti, being mumukṣus, worship him — 'they', the wise (dhīrāḥ), endowed with discriminative intellect, 'transcend this śukra' — this well-known seed of man, the material cause of the body — and do not again creep into a womb. As the śruti has it, 'he sports nowhere any more' (na punaḥ kva ratiṃ karoti). The intent therefore is: such a one ought to be worshipped.
MD_C03_S02_V02: He who, brooding on them, longs after objects of desire, is born again with those very desires here and there. But for one whose desires are wholly fulfilled, who is perfected in the Self, all desires here itself dissolve away. (2)
MD_C03_S02_V02::block-0:
The text now exhibits that, for the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), the renunciation of desire is itself the principal means: 'He who longs for desires (kāmān)' — for the objects of seen and unseen relish — 'brooding upon them' (manyamānaḥ), that is, dwelling on their qualities, praying for them — 'he is born along with those very desires' (kāmabhiḥ), namely the cravings for objects which are themselves the cause of dharma- and adharma-pravṛtti. 'There and there' (tatra tatra) — wherever the desires set the man to deeds for the gaining of objects, there, in the midst of those very objects, he is born swathed by those very desires.

But he 'whose desires are wholly fulfilled' (paryāpta-kāmaḥ) by the cognition of the supreme reality, in whom, by reason of his being one whose desire is the Self alone (ātma-kāma), the desires are 'fully attained on every side' (pari samantataḥ āptāḥ kāmāḥ) — for that paryāpta-kāma, who is also kṛtātmā (one whose Self has been wrought), that is, in whom the Self, having been led away from its non-original avidyā-form, has been wrought through vidyā into its own supreme nature — for him 'here itself' (iha eva), even while abiding in the body, 'all' the springs of dharma- and adharma-pravṛtti 'utterly dissolve' (pravilīyanti), that is, attain dissolution, perish. Since the cause of their birth is destroyed, the desires no more arise. This is the import.
MD_C03_S02_V03: This Self is not gained by exposition, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Whom the Self chooses, by him alone is It gained; to him this Self reveals Its own form. (3)
MD_C03_S02_V03::block-0:
(Pūrvapakṣa intimated:) If, then, the highest gain of all gains is the gain of the Self, then for the sake of that gain the means — exposition (pravacana) and the rest — should be plied in abundance. To this expectation the text replies. — 'This Self', who has been expounded, whose attainment is the supreme goal of man, 'is not gained by exposition' (na pravacanena labhyaḥ), that is, not by mere abundance of veda-śāstrādhyayana. Likewise 'not by intellect' (na medhayā) — by the power of grasping and retaining the meaning of texts; 'nor by much hearing' (na bahunā śrutena), that is, not even by abundance of śravaṇa.

By what then is It gained? The text says: 'Whom alone' — that is, the supreme Self alone — 'this knower' (eṣaḥ vidvān) 'chooses' (vṛṇute), that is, longs to attain — 'by that very choosing (varaṇa) this supreme Self is gained, not by any other means' — for It is by nature ever-attained (nitya-labdha-svabhāva). What sort of attainment of the Self is this for the knower? It is told: 'to him this Self reveals (vivṛṇute) Its own — supreme — body' (svām parām tanūm), that is, Its own ātma-tattva, Its essential form, hidden by avidyā — manifests it forth, just as light, when present, manifests pots and the like that exist already. Therefore the means to the gaining of the Self is solely the relinquishment of all else and the supplication for the Self. This is the meaning.
MD_C03_S02_V04: This Self is not gained by one without strength, nor through heedlessness, nor through tapas devoid of the mark (of saṃnyāsa). The wise man, who strives with these means, his Self enters the abode that is Brahman. (4)
MD_C03_S02_V04::block-0:
These auxiliaries to the supplication for the Self are also stipulated: bala (strength), apramāda (non-heedlessness), and tapas joined with the liṅga, that is, attended with saṃnyāsa. — Inasmuch as 'this Self is not gained by one bereft of strength' (bala-hīnena na labhyaḥ), namely, by him who is destitute of the vigour born of steadfastness in the Self (ātma-niṣṭhā-janita-vīrya); 'nor through heedlessness (pramāda) caused by attachment to worldly objects such as son, cattle, and the like'; likewise 'nor by tapas devoid of the liṅga' (tapaso vāpi aliṅgāt), that is, devoid of the mark.

Here 'tapas' is jñāna; the 'liṅga' is saṃnyāsa. The meaning is: by knowledge that is unaccompanied by saṃnyāsa, It is not gained. 'By these means' (etair upāyaiḥ) — namely, by strength, non-heedlessness, saṃnyāsa, and knowledge — 'whoever, being a wise man (vidvān), a man of viveka, a knower of the Self, strives, being intent thereon — for that learned one this Self enters (viśate) the abode that is Brahman' — fully enters Brahma-dhāma.
MD_C03_S02_V05: Having attained Him, the seers, content in knowledge, perfected in the Self, free from passion, calm — they, the wise, with composed minds, attaining the all-pervading on every side, enter into the All. (5)
MD_C03_S02_V05::block-0:
How does one enter Brahman? It is told: 'Having attained' (samprāpya), having fully realised, 'this Self', the seers (ṛṣayaḥ) — those who possess vision — content (tṛptāḥ) by that very jñāna, and not by any external means of contentment such as serves to nourish the body. They are 'kṛtātmānaḥ' — those whose ātman has been wrought (niṣpanna) into the very form of the supreme Self; 'vīta-rāgāḥ' — from whom rāga and the like blemishes have departed; 'praśāntāḥ' — whose senses are at rest.

Such ones, having attained 'on every side' (sarvataḥ) Him 'who pervades all' (sarva-gam), as ākāśa pervades — not by the upādhi-bound limited fragment, but by realising as ātman that one Brahman without a second (advayam) — they, dhīrāḥ, men of utmost discrimination, yuktātmānaḥ, by nature ever composed, even at the time of the falling of the body 'enter into all' (sarvam evāviśanti); like the ākāśa enclosed in a broken pot, they shed the limitations imposed by avidyā-wrought upādhis. Thus do the knowers of Brahman enter the abode that is Brahman.
MD_C03_S02_V06: Those whose object is well determined by the knowledge born of Vedānta, the strivers of pure being through the yoga of saṃnyāsa — they all, in the worlds of Brahman, at the supreme end, become wholly liberated, with the supreme Immortal as their very Self. (6)
MD_C03_S02_V06::block-0:
Further: 'vedānta-vijñāna' is the cognition arising from the Vedānta texts; the artha (object) of that cognition is the supreme Self to be known; 'those by whom that artha is well determined (su-niścita)' are 'vedānta-vijñāna-su-niścitārthāḥ'. They, by the yoga of saṃnyāsa — that is, by the yoga whose nature is the renunciation of all karman, the yoga consisting of sole steadfastness in Brahman — are 'yatayaḥ' (strivers); they are 'śuddha-sattvāḥ', for by reason of saṃnyāsa-yoga their sattva has been purified.

'They, in the worlds of Brahman' — for ordinary saṃsārins those moments of death are 'aparānta-kālas' (the lower-end times); relative to those, the time of body-shedding at the consummation of saṃsāra for the mumukṣus is 'parānta-kāla', the supreme end. At that supreme end, owing to the multitude of sādhakas, Brahman itself, though one, is figuratively spoken of in the plural as 'brahma-lokeṣu' — manifold-seeming, manifold-attained. Hence the plural; 'in Brahman' is the meaning. They are 'parāmṛtāḥ' — those whose own Self has become the supreme Immortal (param amṛtam), the deathless Brahman; living, they have already become Brahman; thus parāmṛta, 'they all (sarve) are utterly liberated' (parimucyanti), like the extinction of a lamp on every side, like the ākāśa of a broken pot — they reach cessation. They do not stand in need of any further travel to another region.

As the śruti and smṛti say: 'Like the path of birds in the sky, or of an aquatic in water — as no track is seen — such is the going of the wise' (Mahābhārata, Mokṣadharma 181.9), and 'pathless on the paths, they cross to the other shore'. For a region-bounded going belongs only to the realm of saṃsāra, since it is achieved by limited means. But Brahman, being the totality, is not to be reached by any spatial delimitation. For if Brahman were limited by region, it would be like a corporeal substance, having beginning and end, dependent on another, possessed of parts, non-eternal, and a product. Such Brahman cannot be. Therefore its attainment too cannot fittingly be by way of spatial limitation.
MD_C03_S02_V07: The fifteen kalās are gone to their respective supports, all the deities to their respective deities, deeds and the vijñānamaya Self — all alike become one in the supreme imperishable. (7)
MD_C03_S02_V07::block-0:
Moreover, what the knowers of Brahman desire as mokṣa is solely the removal (apanaya) of the saṃsāra-bondage that is avidyā and the rest — not anything that comes about as a kārya (a produced effect). Further: at the time of mokṣa, the kalās — prāṇa and the others which had constituted the body — 'go to their own supports' (svāḥ pratiṣṭhāḥ gatāḥ), that is, return each to its own cause. 'Pratiṣṭhāḥ' is the second-case plural. 'Pañcadaśa' — the fifteen well-known kalās enumerated in the antya-praśna (the closing question of the Praśna Upaniṣad). 'And all the devas' — the body-resident powers stationed in the eye and the other organs — 'go to the prati-devatās', that is, to the sun and the rest, the corresponding presiding deities. And whatever 'karmas' the mumukṣu has performed which have not yet started yielding their fruit (since those that have already started are exhausted only by enjoyment).

The 'vijñānamaya ātman' — having taken on, as ātman, the upādhis fashioned by avidyā such as buddhi, having entered into the differentiated bodies, like the reflection of the sun in water and the like, for the sake of bearing the karmas to their fruit, together with that very vijñānamaya ātman — hence vijñānamaya, that is, predominantly characterised by vijñāna. All these — the karmas and the vijñānamaya ātman — when the upādhi is removed, in the supreme imperishable (pare avyaye), the endless, undecaying Brahman, akin to ākāśa, unborn, unaging, deathless, fearless, without a prior, without a posterior, without inner, without outer, non-dual, auspicious, peaceful — 'all become one' (sarve ekī-bhavanti); they go to non-distinction, attain unity. As the reflections of the sun, when the water-substrates are removed, attain unity in the sun; as the ākāśas of pots, when the pots are removed, attain unity in ākāśa.
MD_C03_S02_V08: Just as rivers, flowing on, reach the ocean and disappear, abandoning name and form — so too the knower, freed from name and form, attains the divine Puruṣa, higher than the high.
MD_C03_S02_V08::block-0:
Furthermore, just as (yathā) rivers (nadyaḥ) — the Gaṅgā and the rest — while flowing onward (syandamānāḥ), proceeding toward their goal, reach the ocean (samudre) and there go to disappearance (astam) — that is, to non-perception, to the state of merging into undifferentiated being (aviśeṣa-ātmabhāvam) — abandoning (vihāya) both name and form (nāmarūpe), so too (tathā) the knower (vidvān), having become freed (vimuktaḥ) from the name-and-form fashioned by avidyā (avidyākṛta-nāma-rūpāt), attains (upaiti) — that is, draws near to — the divine (divyam) Puruṣa, who is higher (param) than even the previously declared akṣara, possessing the characteristics already set forth.

The simile is drawn with care: as the river, while it runs as a river, possesses its distinct name ("Gaṅgā") and its distinct form (the bounded current), and in the ocean these very particulars are extinguished — not because the water is annihilated, but because its individuating limits dissolve into the homogeneous mass of water — exactly so the knower's individuality, which is itself nothing but a product of avidyā, is shed; the substantial being is not lost but stands forth as the undifferentiated Puruṣa. The text declares this fruit to be no mere succession to a higher loka but the very absorption that constitutes videha-mukti.
MD_C03_S02_V09: He, indeed, who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; in his lineage there shall be no one who is not a knower of Brahman. He crosses beyond sorrow, crosses beyond evil, and being released from the knots of the heart's cave, becomes immortal.
MD_C03_S02_V09::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa: It is well known that toward the highest good there are many obstacles. Therefore, even the knower of Brahman, when obstructed at the moment of death by some affliction (kleśa) or by another agent — say, by a deva or the like — might travel along some other path and not become Brahman itself.

Siddhānta: Not so. By vidyā itself every obstruction has been removed. For mokṣa is constituted solely by the removal of the obstruction that is avidyā; it is not the removal of any other obstruction — because liberation is eternal (nityatva) and is one's own very being (ātmabhūtatva). It is not a fresh attainment whose path some agent could intercept; what is one's own nature cannot be barred by another.

Therefore, that one (saḥ) — anyone (yaḥ kaścit) — who, here in the world, knows (veda) that supreme Brahman, who knows directly, "I myself am verily that" (sākṣād aham eva asmi iti), he travels by no other course. Even the devas are unable to set up an obstacle for him with respect to his attainment of Brahman; for he is the very Self (ātmā) of those very devas — and what would obstruct itself? Therefore, knowing Brahman, he becomes Brahman itself.

Further, in the family of this knower (asya viduṣaḥ), no non-knower of Brahman (a-brahmavit) is born — his whole line is purified by the radiance of his knowledge.

Further, he crosses sorrow (śokam) — the mental anguish (mānasaṃ santāpam) caused by the lack of various desired things; even while still living (jīvann eva) he has gone beyond it. This is jīvanmukti. He crosses evil (pāpmānam) — that is, dharma and adharma both, both of which are bondage — and being released from the knots of the cave (guhā-grantibhyaḥ), the knots of avidyā lodged in the heart, when the body falls he becomes immortal. This very point has already been declared: "The knot of the heart is cut" (Mu.U. 2.2.9), and the rest.
MD_C03_S02_V10: This very truth has been declared by a ṛc: "Those who are performers of the rites, learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas), established in Brahman, who themselves offer oblations to the Ekarṣi fire with faith — to them alone should one teach this Brahma-vidyā, and to those by whom the head-vow has been duly observed."
MD_C03_S02_V10::block-0:
Now at this point the upasaṃhāra — the conclusion — is being made by exhibiting the rule (vidhi) for the proper transmission (sampradāna) of Brahma-vidyā. "This very rule for the imparting of vidyā has been illumined (abhyuktam) by a ṛc, by the mantra."

Kriyāvantaḥ — those endowed with the performance of the prescribed rites (yathokta-karmānuṣṭhāna-yuktāḥ); for action (karman), where qualified, has its place as antecedent purification, not as direct cause of the knowledge of Brahman.

Śrotriyāḥ — versed in śruti.

Brahmaniṣṭhāḥ — devoted to the lower Brahman (apare brahmaṇi abhiyuktāḥ), seekers ardent to know the supreme Brahman (paraṃ brahma bubhutsavaḥ). Note Śaṅkara's careful samāsa-vigraha: brahma-niṣṭhāḥ here designates not those who already abide in para-Brahman (for the very vidyā that effects such abiding is what is being given), but those whose niṣṭhā is upon apara-Brahman as a preparatory upāsanā, and who are now turned outward, hungering for the para.

Svayam ekarṣiṃ juhvate — those who themselves (svayam) offer oblations into the fire named Ekarṣi (ekarṣi-nāmānam agnim juhvati), being faithful (śraddadhānāḥ). This is a particular Atharvan rite.

To these alone — those who are saṃskṛtātman, refined of soul, fit vessels (pātrabhūtānām) — should one teach this Brahma-vidyā: vadeta, brūyāt.

Śirovratam — the vow consisting in carrying fire upon the head (śirasi agni-dhāraṇa-lakṣaṇam), as the veda-vrata of the Ātharvaṇas is well known. Yaiḥ tu — and those by whom that vow has been observed (cīrṇam) duly, as enjoined (yathāvidhānam) — to those alone should one speak it. The restriction is twofold: śīla and adhikāra together; neither rite without learning nor learning without the vow qualifies the recipient.
MD_C03_S02_V11: This is the truth that the ṛṣi Aṅgiras declared of old; one who has not observed the vow does not study it. Salutation to the supreme ṛṣis! Salutation to the supreme ṛṣis!
MD_C03_S02_V11::block-0:
This very (tat etat) — the akṣara, the Puruṣa, the Truth (satyam) — the ṛṣi named Aṅgiras (aṅgirā nāma), formerly (purā), declared (uvāca) to Śaunaka who had duly approached him (vidhivad upasannāya) and questioned him (pṛṣṭavate). The implication (artha): another teacher likewise should expound it to one seeking the highest good, to a mumukṣu seeking liberation, who has duly approached him in due manner — for the sake of mokṣa.

Na etat — "this" — meaning this scriptural body in its written form (grantharūpam) — acīrṇavrataḥ, one who has not undergone the vow, does not even read it (na paṭhati); for only in him by whom the vow has been observed (cīrṇavratasya) does the vidyā become matured (saṃskṛtā) toward fruition. Thus the qualifying restriction is upheld in the very transmission.

The Brahma-vidyā is concluded (samāptā). To those — Brahmā and the others — from whom by the unbroken succession (pāramparya-krameṇa) it has been received, to those supreme ṛṣis (paramarṣibhyaḥ) — salutation (namaḥ). Those Brahmā and the others who have directly seen and known the supreme Brahman (paramaṃ brahma sākṣād dṛṣṭavantaḥ avagatavantaś ca) are the paramarṣis; to them, again, salutation (bhūyo'pi namaḥ).

The twofold utterance (dvir-vacanam) serves two purposes: extreme reverence (atyādara), and the marking of the conclusion of the Muṇḍaka (muṇḍaka-samāpti-artham). Thus the upaniṣad which began by setting forth parā-vidyā and aparā-vidyā as two distinct disciplines, having led the qualified seeker through karma and upāsanā as preparation, through the disclosure of akṣara-Brahman, and through the absorption that is the river-into-the-sea — closes by binding the teaching to the unbroken paramparā in which alone such transmission lives.
